Agentcore Scoping

Validate override endpoint fields through the canonical SSRF guard

The user-supplied mcp_endpoint and sse_endpoint server fields bypassed the URL
guard that proxy_pass_url goes through, even though they are fetched (health
checks, tool discovery, the external scanner subprocess) and interpolated into
generated nginx config exactly like proxy_pass_url. An attacker could register a
server with a benign proxy_pass_url and a mcp_endpoint/sse_endpoint pointing at a
private, loopback, or cloud-metadata address (SSRF), or containing an nginx
metacharacter (config injection).

- Validate mcp_endpoint and sse_endpoint through the same canonical guard as
  proxy_pass_url at the single service-layer chokepoint that every register and
  update/patch write path funnels through, so an alternate endpoint field cannot
  smuggle a private/metadata target or an nginx metacharacter past the primary
  field's check. Empty/unset stays allowed; present-but-invalid is rejected.
- Re-validate the resolved URL before the security scanner spawns its external
  subprocess (which the pinned client cannot protect), with a live DNS lookup so
  a rebound host is caught; a validation failure fails closed as an unsafe scan
  and the subprocess never runs.
- Validate an explicit sse_endpoint / mcp_endpoint before opening the MCP client
  connection and before any stored credential is decrypted or attached.
- Block carrier-grade NAT (100.64.0.0/10, RFC 6598) explicitly in the URL guard
  and the legacy net guard rather than relying on the runtime's is_private
  classification, and pin the range in tests so a runtime change fails loudly.
- Keep the render-time nginx sanitizer as defense in depth.

Adds unit coverage for each path and records the lessons in the security
guidelines.

can instrument the frontend with any observability vendor (Splunk, Datadog,

How it works:
- index.html references <script src="/rum.js">.
- The container entrypoint writes /app/frontend/build/rum.js from the
  RUM_SNIPPET_B64 env var at startup (empty stub when unset, fail-safe).

  before the SPA catch-all so it wins over index.html.

Security guardrails:
- RUM_SNIPPET_B64 is env/secret-only, read-only and masked on the System
  Config page; there is no write API (same trust tier as SECRET_KEY).
- RUM_ALLOWED_HOSTS (optional) rejects any snippet that references a host
  outside the allowlist at startup, failing closed to the empty stub and
  logging only the offending host (never the snippet contents).
- The snippet and allowlist are read from the environment by the writer

Validate skill_name before interpolating it into the registry URL path

The MCPGW server's get_skill_content tool interpolated a user-supplied
skill_name directly into an outbound registry URL path segment after only a
non-empty check. Because this server calls the registry with a privileged
credential, a skill_name such as "../../api/management/iam/users" normalized to
a different registry endpoint and reached it with that privilege — a path
traversal to arbitrary registry APIs.

Validate skill_name against the registry's own canonical skill-name rule
(lowercase alphanumerics in hyphen-separated groups) before building the URL,
anchored so a trailing newline cannot slip through, and reject anything that is
not a single safe identifier with the handler's existing error shape (no request
is made). Add defense-in-depth on the resource_path query value (reject absolute
or traversal sequences). The other registry calls in this server use static
paths or pass user input via the request body, so no other path-segment sink
needs validation.

Adds unit coverage for valid names, traversal/encoded/non-identifier rejections,
and the resource_path guard, and records the lesson in the security guidelines.

Reject reserved wildcard names in server-path / scope writes

A server registered at reserved path /all (or /*) escalated to cross-server
access to every server: the path normalizes (lstrip) into a scope 'server'
value, and 'all'/'*' are the wildcard sentinels the scope resolver promotes to
a full cross-server wildcard.

- validate_server_path (url_guard) rejects reserved names at the registration
  chokepoint, case-insensitive, exact-match (adjacent names like all-tools and
  root path / stay valid).
- add_server_scope refuses a reserved server_name (fail closed, no write).
- import_group scans server_access for a reserved server rule and refuses
  unconditionally (the direct-write sink that skips add_server_scope).
- Read-side _WILDCARD_VALUES and write-side reject sets cross-referenced.

root allowed, both scope-write sinks fail closed with no-write assertions.

fix(mcpgw): allow reverse-proxy Host so airegistry-tools stays healthy

FastMCP 3.x (adopted in #1021 for multi-replica/stateless-http support) enables
host/origin DNS-rebinding protection by default, allowing only 127.0.0.1 /
localhost. But mcpgw is always reached through the registry's nginx/auth front
door as Host 'mcpgw-server' (the service name used identically across Docker
Compose, ECS Service Connect, and Kubernetes). FastMCP rejected that Host with
421 -> the registry health check failed -> nginx dropped the /airegistry-tools/
location block -> clients (e.g. Claude Code) got 405 connecting to the built-in
registry-tools MCP server. Latent since the 1.26.0 cycle.

Fix: configure FastMCP's transport security at startup. The default keeps
protection ON and allowlists 'mcpgw-server' (matching the SSRF guard's
_BUILTIN_PROXY_ALLOWED_HOSTS), so it fixes every deployment surface with no
per-surface config. Operators fronting mcpgw under a different name override the
comma-separated MCPGW_HTTP_ALLOWED_HOSTS; '*' disables protection entirely for
the discouraged unpredictable-Host case.

- servers/mcpgw/server.py: _resolve_allowed_hosts() + wire host_origin_protection
  and allowed_hosts into mcp.run(); MCPGW_HTTP_ALLOWED_HOSTS env (default
  'mcpgw-server').
- tests: 7 unit tests for the resolver, isolated so the shared fastmcp stub
  cannot leak across sibling mcpgw test files.

Verified end-to-end: POST /mcp with Host mcpgw-server:8003 -> 200 (was 421),
bogus Host -> 421 (protection still enforced), airegistry-tools -> healthy,
front-door /airegistry-tools/mcp route restored.

refactor(waf): path-scope the DCR overrides + add MCP flow doc

Split WAF Rule 1 (CommonRuleSet) into two priority-ordered rules with
mutually-exclusive scope-downs:

- Rule 1 (`CommonRuleSet`): managed group at full Block, scope-down =
  NOT starts_with('/realms/mcp-gateway/clients-registrations/'). Every
  non-DCR request runs the full CommonRuleSet, including all 4
  EC2MetaDataSSRF_* sub-rules at Block.
- Rule 2 (`CommonRuleSetForDcr`): same managed group with count-mode
  overrides for EC2MetaDataSSRF_BODY + GenericRFI_BODY, scope-down =
  starts_with('/realms/mcp-gateway/clients-registrations/'). Applies
  only to the Keycloak anonymous DCR endpoint.

This narrows the earlier WebACL-wide override (which counted _COOKIE,
_URIPATH, _QUERYARGUMENTS too, restoring free SSRF defense on those
fields on all paths) and closes the shadow-fix gap where GenericRFI_BODY
started blocking DCR bodies containing 127.0.0.1 / 169.254.169.254 once
EC2MetaDataSSRF_BODY was downgraded.

ManagedRuleGroupStatement must be a rule's top-level statement in WAFv2
(cannot be nested under AndStatement/NotStatement), so the path condition
is expressed via the managed group's own scopeDownStatement.

Rules 3 (KnownBadInputs), 4 (IPRateLimit) and 5 (GlobalRateLimit)
unchanged; priorities renumbered from 2/3/4.

Add per-type authorization scopes for custom entities

Custom entity records were the only first-class asset without a per-type
permission layer: create was ungated (any authenticated user could create
records of any type) and discovery was not type-gated. This brings them to
parity with servers/agents.

- Each type mints list/create/modify/delete_<type>_entity scopes that gate
  discovery + mutation, layered on top of the existing per-record
  owner/visibility checks (defense-in-depth).
- Route gates: view (list/get/rate) 404s the type when the caller lacks the
  list scope (hide existence); mutate (create/modify/delete) 403s. Admin is the
  catch-all bypass. Fails closed on missing permissions.
- Search/discovery applies the type-level gate before per-record visibility, so
  no list scope means zero records of that type, including public ones.
- Type create mints the scope set to mcp-registry-admin (fatal on failure);
  type delete sweeps it from all groups; both trigger a scope reload.

Dynamic-permission naming safety: admin is derived from mutating-prefix
UI-permissions granted for 'all', so a create_<type>_entity scope would
naively confer admin. The admin-derivation rule now runs through a single
shared predicate (privileged_constants.is_admin_conferring_action) that
excludes per-type entity mutation scopes; both the per-request admin check and
the privileged-write guard use it so they cannot drift. Minted mutating actions
equal the excluded set (runtime-asserted); type names are charset-constrained so
a scope key is always a safe field path.

Frontend: the IAM group editor renders per-type scope keys grouped by type,
enumerated from registry config, shown only when custom types are enabled.

Adds a one-time idempotent backfill script for pre-existing types (grants their
scopes to mcp-registry-admin; dry-run by default). After backfill, pre-existing
types are admin-only until an admin grants scopes to other groups.

Add per-record discovery grants for custom entities

Extend the list_<type>_entity scope from a binary type-level gate to a
three-tier grant, reaching parity with list_agents:

- "all" or the bare type name open the whole type (unchanged, backward
  compatible with existing grants and the backfill).
- a record path /<type>/<uuid> opens just that record.

An admin can now grant a group specific records of a custom type, not only
the whole type. Enforced consistently across every read surface: the
collection list intersects the granted paths with the per-record visibility
filter, single-record GET/rate check the specific path, and search checks
each hit's own path. Granting one record never exposes other (even public)
records of the type; the discovery grant and the record's own visibility
must both pass (defense-in-depth, matching agents).

Naming logic lives in two predicates in custom_entity_scopes

fix: normalise nginx location paths to trailing slash (#1501)

MCP server location blocks were generated as `location /path` (no trailing
slash), which nginx treats as a prefix match against any URL starting with
that string. A server registered at a short path such as `/a` would silently
intercept `/api/...`, `/auth`, and other browser/API routes and subject them
to `auth_request /validate`, returning 401 for unauthenticated requests.

Normalise the path with `path.rstrip("/") + "/"` so `location /a/` only
matches the `/a/` subtree. MCP clients (`/server-name/mcp`, `/server-name/sse`)
are unaffected; a bare `GET /server-name` gets nginx's standard 301 to the
trailing-slash form.

fix: guard Entra logout URL length to avoid AADSTS90015 (#1502)

Entra ID rejects logout requests whose URL is too long (AADSTS90015,
"QueryStringTooLong"). Users in many groups get large ID token JWTs, so
appending id_token_hint to the logout URL can breach Entra's limit and the
logout is rejected, leaving a dangling IdP session while the local session
is already cleared.

The Entra branch now drops the optional id_token_hint when the full composed
logout URL (scheme+host+path+query) would exceed MAX_LOGOUT_URL_LENGTH. Entra
still terminates the session via its own SSO cookie; the only visible effect
is a possible account-selection prompt for multi-account users.

Scoped to Entra: Keycloak and Okta do not inline group GUIDs into the id_token
by default and have no equivalent hard rejection, and dropping the hint on
Keycloak would trigger its logout-confirmation page. Both sibling branches now
carry comments explaining why they need no guard.

fix: reject empty server paths that would render as gateway-wide location /

Extends the trailing-slash normalisation (#1501) to close the sibling
gaps and the degenerate-path footgun it surfaced:

- Apply the same trailing-slash normalisation to virtual-server location
  blocks. A bare location /virtual/dev prefix-matched unrelated routes
  like /virtual/devtools, hijacking them into the /validate auth
  subrequest; location /virtual/dev/ only matches the subtree.
- Reject slashes-only server paths (/, //) in validate_server_path. After
  the trailing-slash normalisation these render as a gateway-wide
  location / block that subjects every URL to /validate and shadows the
  static catch-all. No real server registers at the root; fail closed.
- Mirror the rejection at the render boundary
  (_generate_transport_location_blocks) and in the scope-repository sink
  guards (add_server_scope + import_group), so a caller that bypasses the
  registration guard still cannot inject a degenerate row. Broaden and
  rename the import scan to _server_access_has_invalid_server_rule (agent
  rules, which carry no server key, still import).
- Correct the location-block comment: nginx does not auto-301 a bare path
  for a proxy_pass location; it falls through to the catch-all, which is
  safe because connect/discovery URLs always include the /mcp or /sse
  suffix.

fix: internalize OAuth2 logout id_token_hint via server-to-server call (#1503)

The logout flow redirected the browser to the public auth-server URL with
the OIDC id_token_hint JWT embedded in the query string. WAFs and reverse
proxies routinely block long/JWT-looking query strings, returning 403 before
the auth-server was reached -- logout then failed silently after the local
session had already been cleared. The JWT also leaked into browser history
and access/proxy logs while it was being actively revoked.

The registry now calls auth-server's /oauth2/logout/ directly over the
internal network (settings.auth_server_url, the same URL already used by
get_oauth2_providers) and redirects the browser straight to the IdP logout
URL returned in the Location header. The JWT only ever appears on the direct
browser->IdP hop, bypassing the deployment's public infrastructure. This is
deployment-agnostic: auth_server_url is configured and reachable in every
mode (EKS, Docker/Compose, ECS, EC2, local).

- routes.py: server-to-server logout with X-Forwarded-Host/Proto forwarded so
  auth-server's redirect_uri same-origin validation approves the URI;
  _is_safe_logout_redirect guards the returned Location; fail-closed to /login
  on any S2S failure, non-3xx, or unsafe Location; 5s timeout. Logout URL
  length remains owned by auth-server (#1502/#1508); no duplicate guard here.
- auth_server: _is_redirect_within_cookie_domain strips the port from a
  forwarded Host before the same-origin comparison, so a forwarded
  "localhost:7860" matches the port-stripped redirect_uri hostname.
- nginx: /oauth2/logout/ is no longer browser-facing; return 404 to close the
  path that would otherwise let a crafted request reintroduce the JWT into a
  browser-facing URL and the access/WAF logs.
- docs: session-flow logout section rewritten for the S2S flow.
- tests: S2S logout flow (all failure modes) and the host-with-port
  same-origin validation.

fix(egress): ride out transient Vault blips on token save, surface hard failures

The per-user egress token store (OpenBaoStore) only retried on expired-token
errors. Transient Vault/OpenBao unavailability -- HTTP 5xx "local node not
active but active cluster node not found", "connection refused", read timeouts,
all of which occur for a few seconds while an HA cluster re-elects a leader
after a pod restart (eviction / rollout / spot reclaim) -- fell straight
through as a SecretStoreError. When that hit a consent's put_token, the token
was never vaulted and the user was left with a silent "0 tools" and no signal
to retry.

- store: add `_is_transient_error` and extend `_run` with a bounded exponential
  backoff retry (0.5/1/2/4s) for transient errors, kept disjoint from the
  existing single re-auth path. Reads and writes both ride out a leader
  election instead of failing.
- egress callback: catch SecretStoreError separately from EgressAuthError and
  return a clear, retryable "Connection not saved" page (503) instead of a raw
  500 -- and never the success page, so a failed write can't masquerade as a
  connected account.
- tests: cover transient retry-then-persist (write + read), bounded give-up,
  and that non-transient errors are not retried.

fix(egress): vend legacy-principal tokens + migrate to canonical id

The egress vault keys each per-user connection on a principal id resolved
by `_canonical_egress_user` -- the OIDC `sub` when present, else the login
username/email. Connections vaulted before that resolution moved to the
`sub` (across the browser-consent and bearer-vend paths) live under the
OLD username/email key. After the cutover the vend keys on `sub`, misses
the old entry entirely, and the user sees "0 tools" despite holding a
valid, non-expired token -- with no self-service fix but a full re-consent
of every server. It hits users progressively, as each one's session/token
refreshes and flips their resolved id from email to `sub`.

Add a one-hop legacy-key fallback with migrate-on-read to `get_valid_token`:
when the canonical lookup misses and a distinct `legacy_user_id` is given,
read once under the legacy id; on a hit, copy the entry to the canonical
key and delete the legacy one (both best-effort -- a transient store blip
still serves the token and retries the move next vend; a failed delete
leaves a harmless orphan), then serve it. The vend route passes the token's
`sub` claim (== the login username/email that `mint_mcp_proxy_token` stamps
as `subject`) as the legacy id; the canonical `egress_user` claim stays the
primary. Equal ids (older tokens with no `egress_user` claim) are a no-op.

`list_connections` gains the same legacy fallback (merge both buckets,
canonical wins on collision) so the Connected-Accounts UI shows every
connection, and `disconnect` now revokes under both ids. No re-consent
required; the migration is transparent and self-healing.

Adds TestLegacyPrincipalFallback covering migrate-on-hit, canonical-hit
leaves legacy untouched, no-op when legacy is absent/equal, copy-failure
still serves the legacy token, list merge (canonical wins), and dual delete.

test(egress): cover legacy-migrate delete-failure + empty-legacy paths

Raise patch coverage to 100%: add a delete-failure case (copy succeeds,

distinct-but-empty legacy-id case (fallback entered, legacy also misses ->
clean None). Covers _migrate_legacy_entry's delete-except branch and the
legacy-is-None short-circuit in get_valid_token.

fix(egress): stamp OIDC sub as egress_user on self-signed user tokens

A gateway-issued self-signed USER token (generate_user_token) carries
sub=login-username, not the OIDC sub. When a Cursor/Claude bearer minted
from a browser login vends an egress token, _canonical_egress_user resolved
the username and keyed the vault on it, while the browser-consent path keyed
on the OIDC sub. Same human, two vault buckets -> the vend misses the
consented token and the client shows 0 tools, consistently, for whichever
server was consented via the portal.

Thread the session's persisted OIDC sub out of _reconcile_context_against_session
and stamp it as the token's egress_user claim; make _canonical_egress_user
prefer that claim so the vend keys the SAME id the consent path wrote.
Combined with the legacy-principal fallback (this PR), older username-keyed
entries are migrated on read.

test(egress): cover egress_user stamping on session-backed mint

Session-backed /internal/tokens mint stamps the session OIDC sub as the

fix(security): command injection via exec() in token refresh util

The `refreshTokens` function uses `execAsync` to run a shell script. The `projectRoot` parameter is directly interpolated into the command string (`cd "${root}" && ./credentials-provider/generate_creds.sh ...`). Bound cardinality of attacker-influenced Prometheus metric labels

Request-derived values flowed verbatim into Prometheus/OTel metric labels
with no charset normalization, length cap, or cardinality bound. A client
sending randomized values (tool names, JSON-RPC methods, client name/version,
search queries) could explode the emitted time-series count and exhaust
Prometheus memory/storage -- a denial of service affecting every scraped
service. Arbitrary dimension keys on a direct POST could likewise flood the
label-name axis.

Bound both axes, at every emission path, failing bounded by default:

- Ingest normalization (nginx lua): emit_metrics.lua charset-normalizes and
  length-caps tool_name, client_name, and method before buffering. Illegal
  characters become underscores; values truncate to 64 chars. The slash is
  preserved so tools/call and namespaced tool names survive (safe in a label
  value), and the tools/call branch compares the raw method so routing is
  unaffected.

- Value axis (metrics-service processor): a per-process cardinality limiter
  charset-normalizes, length-caps, and distinct-value-caps the attacker-
  influenced dimensions (tool_name, client_name, client_version, query,
  method). Once a configurable maximum distinct count is reached, further
  values collapse to a single "_other" overflow bucket; empties map to a
  distinct "_unset" sentinel.

- Name axis (metrics-service processor): each metric type that emits labels
  has a fixed allowlist of permitted dimension keys, taken from the union of
  what every legitimate emitter sends. Keys outside the allowlist are dropped
  before becoming label names, and metric types with no labelled instrument
  emit no dimension labels at all, so a direct authenticated POST cannot
  invent arbitrary label names.

- In-process (OTel-native) path: the auth server emits tool-execution metrics
  straight to an in-process instrument (the default path), bypassing the
  processor. A shared limiter in registry/observability/label_bounding.py now
  bounds tool_name/method/client_name/client_version there before they reach
  the instrument. The registry's own OTel path already drops every attacker-
  derived attribute, so it needed no change.

The shared limiter is the canonical helper for the in-process path (registry
and auth server import it). The metrics-service processor keeps its own
equivalent because it is a separate deployable that cannot import registry;
the two are kept in sync by mirror-image pin tests that fail if either side's
charset or sentinels drift.

Defaults are configurable via METRICS_MAX_LABEL_CARDINALITY (150) and
METRICS_MAX_LABEL_LENGTH (64); a missing, malformed, or non-positive value
falls back to the default so a misconfiguration bounds rather than disables
the protection.

Adds tests covering value-flood collapse, charset/length normalization,
slash preservation, the key allowlist (unknown keys dropped, unlabelled types
emitting nothing, every legitimate emitter dimension surviving), the
in-process auth path, and cross-limiter semantic parity.

Prevent silent suppression of audit records

Two authenticated callers could make a security-relevant action leave no
audit trail. Both are closed here.

Client-controlled audit key. The audit collection enforces a unique
composite index on (request_id, log_type). The registry audit middleware
and the auth-server /validate handler used the client-supplied
X-Request-ID header verbatim as request_id, and the repository swallowed
the resulting DuplicateKeyError with only a debug log. A caller could log
a benign request under a chosen X-Request-ID, then reuse the same id on a
malicious request of the same log_type; the second insert collided with
the unique index and was silently dropped. The header was neither
format-validated nor regenerated at the edge, so the caller fully
controlled the durable audit key.

Always mint a fresh server-side UUID for the audit key so it cannot be
influenced by the client, and keep the client-supplied
X-Request-ID / X-Correlation-ID only as a sanitized, non-key correlation
field (charset-validated and length-capped, dropped when malformed so raw
or hostile input is never stored). A duplicate-key collision on a
server-generated id is now an audit-integrity event logged at CRITICAL
rather than silently ignored; the insert still returns success so an
audit write never fails the request path. Records for one request under
distinct log_type values still coexist, and endpoint-level producers that
already generated their own UUIDs are unaffected. Also sanitize the
batch-submit correlation id derived from the same header.

The same sanitization now covers the token-mint carrier. The client
X-Correlation-ID flows through /api/tokens/generate into the auth-server
token-mint audit record; that value was previously stored raw and
unbounded. Sanitize it where the registry forwards the header and again
where the auth server consumes the request correlation id (so direct
/internal/tokens callers are covered too), and cap the correlation_id
field on the audit record models so no future producer can persist an
unbounded, arbitrary-charset value. The correlation-id charset check is
anchored with a full match so a value carrying an embedded newline can
never slip through.

Health-substring skip. The audit middleware skipped logging for
health-check traffic using a "/health" substring test on the request
path. Server management routes embed the caller-chosen server path in the
request URL, so a server registered under the name "health" let mutating
admin actions (toggle, edit, rescan, auth-credential updates) carry
"/health" in their URL and be dropped from the audit trail.

Match the known monitoring endpoints exactly (plus the /api/health
sub-tree by prefix) instead of any path that merely contains "/health",
so a management-plane mutation is always audited while genuine health
checks stay suppressed. As defense in depth, reserve the monitoring-route
names (health and friends) at server registration so a shadowing path
cannot be created in the first place; these are kept separate from the
cross-server wildcard reservations.

Harden the metrics-service admin surface

The metrics-service admin surface had two related weaknesses that let a
low-privilege or malformed request destroy stored data.

Authorization: every /admin/* route (retention preview, cleanup, policy
read, policy update, database stats, database size) was guarded only by the
same X-API-Key that ingest clients use, so any valid metrics key -- including
one issued to an ingest-only client or a leaked/shared key -- could perform
admin operations. Admin routes now require a separate, explicitly-configured
admin credential (METRICS_ADMIN_API_KEY) checked by a dedicated dependency
using a constant-time comparison. Ingest keys are rejected on /admin/*, and
the admin surface fails closed: if the admin key is unset, empty, whitespace,
or too short, /admin/* denies rather than falling back to accepting an ingest
key. The admin key must be a high-entropy value of at least 32 characters and
is rejected if it matches a known weak/placeholder value, matching the pepper
validator via a shared helper. It must be configured distinct from ingest
keys; the managed deployment surfaces generate it independently so those
deployments are distinct by construction.

Requiring METRICS_ADMIN_API_KEY is a breaking change: docker-compose upgraders
must add it to .env (unset -> 503 on /admin/*), and admin scripts that used an
ingest key must switch to the admin key (now 401). Terraform and CDK provision
it automatically. See docs/data-retention.md for the upgrade note.

Retention range validation: the retention-policy update accepted any integer
day count. A zero or negative value pushed the cleanup cutoff to the current
instant or into the future, turning the "delete rows older than the cutoff"
query into a full-table wipe. retention_days is now validated at the route
(rejected before any mutation), in the RetentionPolicy constructor and the
policy-update path. When the cutoff is computed the effective day count is
clamped to a safe past floor (never below the minimum retention window), so an
in-memory-corrupted value can only ever reach rows older than that floor rather
than deleting data inside the retention window. Policies loaded from the
database are re-validated and unsafe rows are skipped, so a value persisted by
an older build cannot silently drive a destructive cleanup.

Configuration for the new admin key is wired into the metrics-service env
example, the root env example, both Docker Compose files, the Terraform ECS
module, and the CDK observability construct, with placeholders only.

Tests assert the security properties: an ingest key is rejected on every
admin route, the admin key is accepted, the admin surface denies when no
admin key is configured, ingest authentication is unchanged, and out-of-range
retention values are rejected before any state changes.

fix(nginx): verify IdP upstream TLS to close MITM auth bypass

The nginx reverse-proxy locations for the IdP front-channels reached the IdP
over TLS without verifying its certificate. The PingFederate locations (/as/
token exchange, JWKS, /.well-known/openid-configuration, /pf/, /ext/, /idp/,
/assets/) set proxy_ssl_verify off unconditionally, and the Keycloak locations
(/keycloak/, /realms/, /resources/) set no proxy_ssl_verify directive at all
and relied on nginx's insecure default-off. Because PINGFEDERATE_BASE_URL and
KEYCLOAK_URL can both be https, upstream certificate verification stayed off
even over TLS, letting a machine-in-the-middle between nginx and the IdP
substitute the JWKS (forge tokens) or intercept the token exchange - an
authentication bypass for every user of that IdP.

Enforce verification fail-closed for both upstreams through one shared helper.
Each IdP location now carries a proxy_ssl placeholder that the config generator
renders from the upstream scheme: for an https upstream it emits
proxy_ssl_verify on with proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate, verify depth, and
SNI/hostname pinning to the configured IdP host; for an http upstream it emits
only a comment and logs a plaintext warning, and never emits proxy_ssl_verify
off. The CA bundle paths are operator-configurable via PINGFEDERATE_CA_BUNDLE
and KEYCLOAK_CA_BUNDLE (defaults under the nginx certs mount); a missing bundle
makes nginx reject the upstream cert rather than trust it.

The URL parse now reads the scheme and host before resolving the port, so a
malformed (out-of-range) port in an https IdP URL falls back only the port to
the scheme default and keeps the intended https scheme, instead of silently
downgrading to the unverified http branch. A genuinely broken URL is left for
nginx -t to reject rather than degrading to no-verify.

The change is applied identically to both nginx templates (http-only and
http+https, including the per-listener duplicated blocks). Adds unit tests for
each renderer, an end-to-end test that the proxy_ssl placeholder is actually
substituted in the rendered config, a guard that a malformed port preserves the
https scheme, and grep-based guards asserting neither conf disables TLS
verification on a PingFederate or Keycloak location, plus docs for the new
CA-bundle requirements in .env.example, docs/idp/pingfederate.md, and the
security guidelines.

   registry->auth-server call, auth-server reconstructs the request origin as the
   internal scheme/host (http/loopback) and the forwarded headers do not survive, so a

   extra setup (imported realm sets post.logout.redirect.uris='+' + redirectUris

   <host>/logout must be registered on the app client. docs/idp/cognito.md corrected: it

   error string.

fix(secrets): retry overflow reads that race a generation cleanup

get_token / list_for_user could read the root at generation G1, then a
concurrent same-principal commit flips the manifest to G2 and deletes G1's
shards before the reader fetches them. The shard read used required=True and
surfaced a hard SecretStoreError on the resulting 404 -- a transient error on a
no-retry read path (it gates token vend for a live proxied request).

generation (or an inline/empty layout). Handle it as such:

  _StaleShardError when a required shard is absent, distinguishing "cleaned up
  because the manifest already moved on" from a genuinely corrupt layout.

  that re-reads the root and retries, logging at INFO when a race is observed.
  After exhausting retries it raises a clear SecretStoreError.

root and deletes the old shards mid-read; both get_token and list_for_user
recover. Verified the tests fail against the pre-fix required=True behavior.

fix(egress): fall back to JWT exp when token response omits expires_in

Providers like Salesforce omit expires_in from the token response but issue a
JWT access token bounded by an exp claim. _expires_at previously returned None
in that case, so expires_at stayed unset, the vend path treated the token as
long-lived, and the single-flight refresh never fired -- the gateway kept
injecting a token the upstream had already expired ("Invalid token").

Decode the access token's exp as a best-effort, unsigned fallback (opaque or
malformed tokens -> None). Applied at _to_stored_token so it covers both the
exchange_code and refresh_token paths.

fix(egress): apply transient-failure hardening to the token vend read path

PR #1490 hardened the consent-callback WRITE path against transient
Vault/OpenBao unavailability (bounded retry + a clear 503 "Connection not
saved"). The token-vend READ path (auth-server -> /_egress_internal/egress-token
-> registry -> OpenBao) did not get the same treatment: after the registry
exhausts its retry budget the vend fails, the auth-server returns None and falls
through to a TOKENLESS upstream call, which 401s. That is the same silent-failure
class the write-path fix removed, just on the read side. Follow-up requested by
@aarora79 on #1490.

Two coupled gaps addressed:

- Timeout <-> retry-budget coupling made explicit. The auth-server vend call used
  a hard-coded timeout=10.0 while the registry's transient-retry budget is ~7.5s;
  the two were implicitly coupled and could silently drift. Expose
  registry.secrets.openbao.store.transient_retry_budget_seconds() as the single
  source of truth and derive the vend timeout from it (+ headroom) in
  auth_server.server._egress_vend_timeout_seconds().

- Read-path graceful failure mirroring the write-path 503. The registry vend
  endpoint now catches SecretStoreError from get_valid_token and returns 503
  (instead of a 500 / opaque miss). The auth-server classifies transport
  failures/timeouts and 5xx as transient, raising EgressVendUnavailable, and the
  mcp_proxy hop returns a retryable 503 (JSON-RPC error, Retry-After) instead of
  forwarding tokenless. Terminal denials (401/403/404) keep their existing
  behavior.

Tests: registry vend returns 503 on store failure; store budget helper;
_vend_egress_token transient classification (transport/timeout/5xx raise;
401/403/404 -> None; 200 -> body); timeout > retry budget; mcp_proxy returns a
retryable 503 on transient vend failure.

fix(egress): authorize forwarded body before the egress vend (TM-15 ordering)

Addresses @aarora79's review on #1529.

The transient-vend hardening introduced an ordering hazard: in mcp_proxy the
egress vend ran before the forwarded-body scope re-authorization. While OpenBao
is briefly unavailable the vend raises EgressVendUnavailable and the proxy
returns a retryable 503, short-circuiting before the 403 scope check. An
authorization denial was therefore masked by a transient-availability signal --
an unscoped caller got "503 retry later" instead of "403 denied", and a genuine
denial could look like a transient blip in logs/metrics. It also broke the
pre-existing TM-15 test (test_forwarded_body_reauthorized_denies_unscoped_caller).

Move _authorize_forwarded_mcp_body to run BEFORE the egress block, so a scope
denial is always 403 regardless of vend / OpenBao availability, and no outbound
work (vend or upstream forward) happens for an unauthorized caller. Authorized
callers are unaffected: the connected egress/obo paths already passed this same
re-auth downstream, so anyone with the server's scopes still reaches the vend
and the consent/local-answer paths.

Tests:

  EgressVendUnavailable, and the vend is never attempted.
- The egress consent + obo-terminal + vend-unavailable tests now represent an
  authorized caller (they reach the egress block, which is now behind the scope
  check) via _patch_scope_repo_allow_all.

fix(keycloak): don't assign to reserved $GROUPS in agent setup verify

verify_setup() stored the service account's group list in a variable
named GROUPS. GROUPS is a special bash variable -- an array of the
caller's numeric supplementary group IDs -- so the scalar assignment
fails. The script runs under `set -e`, so it aborts right there, before
printing the group name and before the final summary.

The failure is silent and misleading: the service account, its group
membership, and the groups protocol mapper have all already been created
correctly by the time verify_setup runs, so the setup actually succeeded
-- but the script exits 1 with no error message, and any caller (e.g.
the macOS setup skill's Phase 12) reports the agent creation as failed.

The bug would be latent even without `set -e`: shellcheck also flags two
SC2128 warnings, because expanding the array without an index yields
only its first element, so the group check would compare against a
numeric GID rather than the group names.

Rename the variable to account_groups and declare it local. Verified
against a live Keycloak: the script now completes with exit 0, prints
"Service account is in 'mcp-servers-unrestricted' group", and reaches
the SUCCESS summary. shellcheck drops from 7 findings to 2 (the
remainder is a pre-existing, unrelated SC2034). No other GROUPS=
assignments exist in the setup scripts.

fix(keycloak): derive agent token keycloak_url from env, not a hardcoded host

generate_agent_token() wrote a hardcoded "keycloak_url" into every
generated agent config:

  "keycloak_url": "https://mcpgateway.ddns.net/keycloak",

That is the upstream maintainer's demo deployment. Every field around it
is templated from the environment, so this one looks like a leftover from
manual testing. The effect is that any install -- local, on-prem, or a
different cloud deployment -- gets agent configs pointing at a host it
has no relationship with. Token generation then fails at DNS resolution:

  Failed to make token request to Keycloak:
  HTTPSConnectionPool(host='mcpgateway.ddns.net', port=443):
  Failed to resolve 'mcpgateway.ddns.net'

Read KEYCLOAK_EXTERNAL_URL instead, matching the precedence already used
by credentials-provider/generate_creds.sh, and fall back to $ADMIN_URL --
the URL this script is already successfully driving the Admin API with,
so it is correct by construction. The value must be the external URL
rather than the in-network $KEYCLOAK_URL (http://keycloak:8080), because
the token consumers run on the host, not inside the compose network.

Fixes #1572

fix(keycloak): add the 'basic' scope to agent M2M clients so tokens carry aud=mcp-gateway

create_agent_client() is the only client-creation payload in the repo that
sets "defaultClientScopes" explicitly. Every other client -- mcp-gateway-web,
mcp-gateway-m2m in init-keycloak.sh, and the Python _ensure_client() -- omits
the field and so inherits the realm defaults, which include Keycloak's
built-in 'basic' scope. The agent payload enumerates five scopes and leaves
'basic' out.

That scope is not cosmetic here. init-keycloak.sh attaches two protocol
mappers to it, precisely because it is the one scope reliably present on
every client:

  - setup_dcr_groups_mapper    -> 'groups' claim
  - setup_dcr_audience_mapper  -> aud="mcp-gateway"

Without 'basic', the agent's tokens get neither. The audience mapper is the
one that breaks authentication. auth_server/providers/keycloak.py validates
with verify_aud=True against accepted_audiences of [client_id, m2m_client_id,
"mcp-gateway"], and deliberately excludes "account" -- that is Keycloak's
default audience on every realm token, so accepting it would permit a
same-realm cross-client confused-deputy replay. An agent token therefore
carries aud="account" and is rejected by the gateway it was just created to
call. The comment on setup_dcr_audience_mapper spells out the intent the
agent client is silently opting out of.

The 'groups' claim survives only by accident: create_agent_client attaches
its own oidc-group-membership-mapper directly to the client, duplicating
what 'basic' already provides. That masks the missing scope, since the
token looks correct on inspection until you check 'aud'.

Verified against the tokens generated by a real run of this script:

  aud       : account
  azp       : agent-test-agent-m2m
  auth_time : absent (confirming 'basic' was not attached)

and decoding those same tokens with the gateway's accepted_audiences list
raises InvalidAudienceError. Add 'basic' to the list rather than removing
the explicit block, keeping the change to one line and leaving the
already-working redundant groups mapper alone. bash -n passes.

Note this path is reachable only with #1570 and #1572 fixed; verify_setup()
aborts under `set -e` before token generation, which is why the stale
audience went unnoticed.

Fixes #1573

fix(scopes): correct the inverted group_mappings in the scope seed files

The DocumentDB seed files carry group_mappings arrays that were never
inverted when scopes moved out of auth_server/scopes.yml (removed in
1db1f082). The old YAML was keyed group -> [scopes]; the seed documents are
keyed scope -> [groups]. The migration copied each group's scope list
verbatim into that scope's group list, so the relation is transposed:

  scope                             old YAML groups              seed file
  mcp-servers-unrestricted/read     registry-admins,             []
                                    mcp-registry-admin
  mcp-servers-unrestricted/execute  (same)                       []
  mcp-registry-admin                mcp-registry-admin           mcp-registry-admin,
                                                                 ...unrestricted/read,
                                                                 ...unrestricted/execute

map_cognito_groups_to_scopes inverts these arrays into a group -> scopes
lookup, so the two consequences are:

- The unrestricted scopes have no groups and are unreachable. Every
  administrator resolves to zero server access.
- mcp-registry-admin lists two *scope* ids where group names belong. A
  Keycloak group cannot contain '/', so those entries are inert; they match
  no token claim and grant nothing.

Net effect on a fresh install: an operator in mcp-registry-admin or
registry-admins authenticates, resolves 0 scopes, and is denied server
registration. The documented quickstart cannot complete:

  User service-account-... with 1 groups mapped to 0 scopes
  ... attempted API register without register_service permission
  POST /api/servers/register HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

The same arrays back the login-time session-group filter
(auth_server/group_filter.py), which intersects a user's IdP groups with the
union of every group_mappings array, so a missing group is also dropped from
the session.

Restore the mapping the YAML specified: grant the two unrestricted scopes to
registry-admins and mcp-registry-admin, and drop the inert scope ids. The
Entra admin Object ID is not hardcoded -- init-mongodb-ce.py already appends
it to registry-admins from ENTRA_GROUP_ADMIN_ID.

Self-mapping (scope 'registry-admins' granted to group 'registry-admins') is
intentional throughout this project and left as is; only the transposition is
corrected.

Verified against the running stack. Reseeded, restarted registry and
auth-server, then GET /validate for a service account in mcp-registry-admin:

  before: groups=[mcp-registry-admin, ...] scopes=[]
  after : scopes=[mcp-registry-admin,
                  mcp-servers-unrestricted/read,
                  mcp-servers-unrestricted/execute]

and POST /api/servers/register then succeeds where it returned 403.
Negative control: an agent in only mcp-servers-unrestricted still resolves to
scopes=[], so this restores admin access without widening any other group's
privileges.

Adds tests/security/test_scope_seed_group_mappings.py: static assertions that
no entry is path-qualified (the scope-vs-group confusion), that the privileged
scopes are reachable, and that admin groups reach the unrestricted scopes.
4 of its 10 cases fail on the unfixed seed data. Full suite: 6697 passed,
56 skipped.

Fixes #1574

fix(macos-setup): ask uv for the 3.14 interpreter, not PATH's python3

The Phase 1 check I added gated on `python3 --version` from PATH, but
Phase 5 runs `uv sync`, which resolves uv's own managed interpreters and
never consults PATH. On a machine with system python3 3.13.5 and a
uv-managed 3.14.6, the check reported PYTHON_TOO_OLD and told the operator
to stop -- yet `uv sync` completed successfully and built a 3.14.6 venv.

That is a false failure on exactly the machines where setup works, which is
worse than the original bug: it blocks a working install rather than
deferring an error.

Gate on `uv python find '>=3.14'` instead, which reports what `uv sync`
will actually use. Verified both directions on this machine: PYTHON_OK with
the uv-managed 3.14.6 present, and PYTHON_TOO_OLD under
`--no-managed-python` (system-only, 3.13.5) and for an impossible '>=99.0'.

Also drop the now-unreachable PYTHON_FAIL table row, since the check no
longer emits that token.

Refs #1568

fix(build): make .env secret generation portable; BSD sed -i silently no-ops

build_and_run.sh generated five required secrets (SECRET_KEY,
AUTH_SERVER_NGINX_MARKER_SECRET, DOCUMENTDB_PASSWORD, METRICS_KEY_PEPPER,
OPENBAO_TOKEN) with the same pattern: strip any empty/quoted-empty line with
`sed -i '/re/d' .env`, then append the real value. That sed invocation is not
portable. On BSD/macOS, `sed -i` treats the NEXT argument as a mandatory
backup-file suffix, so `sed -i '/re/d' .env` consumes the script `/re/d` as the
suffix and errors with "unescaped newline inside substitute pattern". The code
swallowed it with `2>/dev/null || true`.

Consequence on macOS: the empty placeholder line was never removed, the
freshly generated value was appended BELOW it, and python-dotenv / compose take
the FIRST assignment -- the empty one. The generator logged "added to .env"
while the effective value stayed empty. For AUTH_SERVER_NGINX_MARKER_SECRET
this crash-loops the auth-server, which fails closed on a required-but-empty
marker (config.py raises: without it the auth_server would mint mcp-proxy
tokens unconditionally). The other four were only masked because a value was
usually already present by the time this ran.

Replace the five copy-pasted blocks with one `ensure_secret VAR hex_bytes`
helper that rewrites the file with `grep -v` (identical behavior on GNU and BSD)
and appends exactly once. Verified on macOS: an empty line, a quoted-empty
line, and a missing var each end with exactly one populated assignment, and an
operator-provided value is left untouched. bash -n passes.

Found during a full clean-install rebuild via the macos-setup skill, where the
auth-server crash-looped on the empty marker secret until this was fixed.

Fixes #1577

fix(macos-setup): enable the registered server, and document the SSRF allowlist

Two gaps that leave a by-the-book run without a working MCP server.

1. `register` does not enable. server_routes.py indexes a newly registered
   server with is_enabled=False, and a disabled server gets no nginx route, so
   every call to it returns 405 and it does not appear on the dashboard. Phase 15
   registered the Cloudflare server and then only grepped `list` output for the
   name -- which matches a disabled entry too (it lists as `✗ ⚫`). The skill
   claims three times that the server "appears immediately on login"; it does
   not. Add the `toggle --path /cloudflare-docs` step, and make the verification
   check `Enabled: True` / `Health: healthy` plus the generated nginx location
   block rather than mere presence in the list.

2. Registering an in-network server needs an SSRF opt-in. The compose stack runs
   currenttime-server and realserverfaketools-server but the skill never
   registers them, so nothing documented how. Their proxy_pass_url values are
   docker-network hostnames resolving to RFC-1918 addresses, which the health
   checker's SSRF guard blocks by default:

     Health check blocked by SSRF guard for http://currenttime-server:8000/:
     resolves to blocked/private IP 172.18.0.4 (credentials NOT sent)

   They register and enable but stay UNHEALTHY with no route. Add an optional
   subsection covering the whole sequence: set SSRF_ALLOWED_HOSTS, recreate the
   registry container to pick it up, register, toggle, healthcheck. Uses
   SSRF_ALLOWED_HOSTS (named hosts) rather than SSRF_ALLOWED_CIDRS, per the
   guidance in .env.example, so the allowlist does not cover every present and
   future container on the bridge network.

   Note the default-deny is correct and is left alone: the guard cannot
   distinguish a local demo container from an attacker probing internal
   addresses, so internal targets stay opt-in. /airegistry-tools/ is unaffected
   because auth_server treats it as an internal ingress relay
   (_INTERNAL_INGRESS_RELAY_SERVERS).

Both fixes verified against the running stack: /cloudflare-docs, /currenttime/,
and /realserverfaketools/ all report `✓ 🟢 Enabled: True Health: healthy` with
nginx location blocks generated, and real tool calls succeed through the gateway
(current_time_by_timezone returned a live timestamp; quantum_flux_analyzer
returned its simulated payload).

Also fixes the token-file references in the verification commands to use the
${TOKEN_FILE} variable already set in the phase, instead of repeating a
hardcoded filename that Phase 14 never produces (see #1576).

fix(telemetry): prevent silent heartbeat drop in usage-report export

The usage-report bastion export streams whole DocumentDB collections
through mongosh. On the free-tier t2.micro bastion (1 vCPU / 1 GB), the
first (startup) fetch exhausts CPU credits, so the second (heartbeat)
fetch ran credit-throttled and exceeded the 120s mongosh timeout. The
fetch returned 0 documents silently and the export still wrote a CSV and
exited 0, zeroing out the entire Liveness / Engagement / LTV half of the
report with no error.

Fixes at three layers:

- telemetry_db.py: raise the mongosh fetch timeout to 900s; make
  _fetch_documents raise on a timeout/no-output result instead of
  returning an empty list silently; abort cmd_export if any collection in
  a combined export returns 0 rows (near-certain failed fetch, not an
  empty collection).
- run_report.sh: after download, verify the CSV contains both startup and
  heartbeat events and abort (removing the partial CSV) if either is
  missing, so a silent drop can never reach the report.
- terraform: add bastion_instance_type variable, default t3.medium (was a
  hardcoded t2.micro), addressing the root cause. On t3.medium the
  combined export completes in ~27s with both event types intact.

The instance-type bump requires terraform apply to replace the bastion.

fix(cli): forward the custom-OIDC fields so egress-configure --provider custom works

`egress-configure --provider custom` could never succeed. argparse accepted the
flag, but neither the CLI nor RegistryClient.configure_egress_auth forwarded any
of the five custom_* fields, and the server's resolve_provider requires two of
them:

  custom requires custom_authorize_url and custom_token_url

So every attempt failed server-side, and the only way to configure a custom OIDC
provider was to POST /api/servers/{path}/egress-auth directly with curl.

This is a CLI/UI parity gap rather than a deliberate restriction. The API request
model accepts all five fields, EgressOAuthConfig persists four of them, the
frontend server-edit modal already sends custom_authorize_url/custom_token_url
(with its own tests), and list_providers() advertises "custom" as selectable.
Nothing was protected by omitting the flags.

Add the fields to configure_egress_auth and the matching --custom-* flags,
following the existing `if x is not None` convention so an omitted flag sends
nothing and cannot null out a stored value on edit.
--custom-token-auth-style is constrained to post_body|basic_header to match
TokenEndpointAuthStyle.

it: it is the RFC 8707 resource indicator added for Atlassian's Rovo MCP, and
leaving it out would reproduce this same gap for the next per-resource provider.

Motivating case: Salesforce Hosted MCP (Headless 360), whose OAuth endpoints are
per-org (https://<my-domain>.my.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/{authorize,token}).

right mechanism -- and it was unreachable from the CLI.

Verified end to end against a live Salesforce org using ONLY the CLI, after first
resetting the server to --mode none so the write was genuine:

  egress_auth_mode     : oauth_user
  egress_provider      : custom
  scopes               : ['mcp_api', 'refresh_token']
  custom_authorize_url : https://...my.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/authorize
  custom_token_url     : https://...my.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token

org host, scope "mcp_api refresh_token", code_challenge_method=S256, and the
registry's own /oauth2/egress/callback as redirect_uri -- and the server appears
in GET /api/egress-auth/available-servers (the Connected Accounts dropdown).

args through to the client. 4 of the 6 cases fail against current main.

feat(entra): per-server PRM for all servers on Entra to unblock IDE login

Extends the per-server RFC 9728 PRM gate so that on Microsoft Entra EVERY
server -- including plain servers (egress_auth_mode none/unset), not just
obo_exchange / oauth_user -- advertises a per-server PRM whose `resource` is its
exact connection URL.

Why: Entra binds the requested scope to the RFC 8707 `resource` and matches
`resource` to a registered App ID URI exactly. The gateway-wide PRM advertises
the bare origin, which a spec-compliant client (Claude Code, RFC 9728 §3.3)
canonicalizes with a trailing slash; Entra App ID URIs cannot end in a slash, so
the token exchange fails with AADSTS9010010. The only value that satisfies both
the client (resource == the connection URL it is accessing) and Entra (a
slash-free registered App ID URI) is the per-server connection URL. Verified
end-to-end against a live Entra tenant: a plain server (airegistry-tools) now
completes the full PKCE login and connects.

Behavior is unchanged for lenient IdPs (Keycloak/Cognito/Okta/Auth0): plain
servers keep using the bare-origin gateway-wide PRM and need no per-server App
ID URI registration. Only Entra requires the per-server resource and incurs the
per-connection-URL identifierUri registration cost (operator registers each
connection URL as an App ID URI with a user_impersonation scope exposed +
granted to the IDE client; GET /api/egress/obo-identifier-uris lists them).

fix(entra): accept per-server aud with egress off + reject id_token as access token

Addresses review findings on the per-server-PRM-for-Entra change:

The mcp_proxy relays ingress auth to the built-in registry-tools server
(_INTERNAL_INGRESS_RELAY_SERVERS) so it can call the registry API as the
caller. It only relayed the Authorization header, but the gateway carries
the caller bearer in X-Authorization, which _forward_headers stripped
unconditionally. The internal server then received no bearer and failed
with 'Bearer token not found in Authorization or X-Authorization header'.

fix(frontend): derive connect-URL /mcp suffix from append_mcp_path

The connect-URL builder decided the trailing /mcp segment from a heuristic
on the upstream proxy_pass_url (skip append when it ends in /mcp|sse|v1).
That diverged from the server-side PRM resource, which appends /mcp unless
append_mcp_path is explicitly false. For a server whose upstream ends in
/mcp (e.g. Slack) with append_mcp_path unset, the UI emitted /<path> while
the PRM advertised /<path>/mcp, so a spec-compliant client rejected the
config: 'Protected resource .../<path>/mcp does not match expected
.../<path> (or origin)' (RFC 9728).

Default to appending /mcp when append_mcp_path is unset, mirroring the
server-side default so the connection URL always equals the PRM resource.
Explicit append_mcp_path=false (root-endpoint servers) is unchanged. Adds
a regression test for the unset + upstream-ends-in-/mcp case.

fix(a2a): accept percent-encoded ARNs so AgentCore agents are routable

_NGINX_AGENT_URL_SAFE did not allow '%' anywhere in the url path, so every
Bedrock AgentCore A2A agent was silently unroutable through the gateway.

AgentCore invocation urls embed a percent-encoded ARN, and the registry's own
importer builds them that way (cli/agentcore/models.py::build_invocation_url):

  https://bedrock-agentcore.{region}.amazonaws.com/runtimes/{encoded-ARN}/invocations

An ARN cannot sit in a path segment unencoded, so '%' is unavoidable -- and it
is the only character in a real AgentCore url that the old pattern rejected.
One half of the codebase therefore generated urls the other half refused:
_create_agent_location_block raised ValueError("unsafe agent url"), the caller
logged a warning and skipped the agent, and nginx got no location block. Six
imported agents (all enabled and healthy, three with protocol 'a2a') produced
"Generated 0 A2A agent location blocks".

Allow '%' only as a COMPLETE %XX triplet. A bare or truncated '%' still fails,
and the characters that would break out of a location block (`}`, `;`,
whitespace, newlines) remain excluded because they are not hex digits, so the
anti-injection guarantee the pattern exists for is unchanged.

Boundary cases checked rather than assumed. Rejected: '%', '%2', '%zz', '%2y',
';return 1', '}', embedded newline, whitespace, 'ftp://'. Accepted: the real
AgentCore url, plain https, bare docker names with ports, mixed-case hex.

Note '%0A%0D' (encoded CRLF) is accepted by the triplet rule. Verified against
real nginx that this cannot inject config, because proxy_pass treats
percent-escapes as opaque literal text:

  proxy_pass https://example.com/a%0A%0Dadd_header/;
  -> nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful

Verified on a live 1.28.0 stack: "Generated 0 A2A agent location blocks"
becomes "Generated 3", three /agent/* blocks are emitted, `nginx -t` passes,
and the encoded ARN survives verbatim into proxy_pass (re-encoding it would
point the route at a non-existent runtime). End to end, a call through the
gateway now reaches AgentCore itself -- /validate returns 200 and the response
carries x-amzn-ErrorType: MissingAuthenticationTokenException from AWS rather
than a gateway error, i.e. the routing works and only the egress credential is
absent (separate configuration concern).

Adds regression tests: an AgentCore url produces a block with the ARN intact,
four incomplete-escape forms are skipped, and an injection attempt adjacent to
a valid escape is skipped. The positive test fails against current main.
Full suite: 6734 passed, 74 skipped.

fix(health): stream MCP initialize instead of buffering the full response

_initialize_mcp_session used a plain client.post(), which waits for the
response body to complete before returning. A streamable-http MCP server
that keeps the connection open with SSE/chunked framing after sending the
initialize result never satisfies that, so the health check blocks until
HEALTH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS and the server is marked unhealthy even
though it answered correctly (status, session ID) well before then.

Switch to client.stream() and read only the headers, matching what the
session ID actually needs. The failure path still reads the body via
response.aread() for the log line, since a non-streaming error response
is finite and closes normally.

test(health): migrate the log-redaction stub to client.stream

test_health_logs_strip_query_and_response_body still stubbed client.post,
so after the switch to client.stream the mocked 500 response was never
used and response.status_code came back as an auto-generated AsyncMock,
failing the status=500 assertion.

Stubbing client.stream restores that assertion and, more importantly,
puts the secret-bearing response back on the path the logging call
actually sees, so the two redaction assertions from #1564 exercise the
redaction again instead of passing against an empty mock.

fix(health): stream the MCP ping so a held-open response cannot stall the check

Follows #1614, which streamed the initialize hop. The ping hop still used
client.post, so a streamable-http server that answers with
Content-Type: text/event-stream and holds the connection open still stalled
the probe for the whole health-check timeout. The resulting ReadTimeout
surfaced as "unhealthy: ReadTimeout" and the server was dropped from nginx
routing, which is the symptom #1614 set out to fix.

Adds _probe_mcp_endpoint, a single head-only probe shared by both ping call
sites, so the streaming discipline cannot be applied to one hop and forgotten
on another. Only a 400 has its body read: it is the sole status whose payload
decides health (the JSON-RPC -32600 check in _is_mcp_endpoint_healthy_streamable)
and it is a finite response that closes normally. The helper also passes an
explicit timeout so the ping no longer silently inherits a different budget
from the client.

Measured against a server that flushes the session id and then holds the
stream open for 20s, the ping hop goes from a 5.02s ReadTimeout to status 200
in 0.01s.

_try_ping_without_auth keeps client.post: it reads only status_code and is
reached only after initialize already failed, so it never stalls the healthy
path.

test(health): cover both branches of _probe_mcp_endpoint

A live run against 187 real ping responses only ever saw 200 and 404, so
the 400 branch -- the one status whose body decides health via the
JSON-RPC -32600 check -- was exercised nowhere outside the helper itself.
Getting that branch wrong is quiet: .json() on an unread streamed
response raises httpx.ResponseNotRead, which the broad handler would turn
into a bogus "unhealthy" verdict for a server that is actually fine.

Adds one test per branch: the 400 path must await aread() and then judge
healthy, and the 200 path must never touch the body, since that is the
read that hangs against a held-open event stream.

fix(cli): forward append_mcp_path from register --config

POST /api/servers/register accepts append_mcp_path as a form field and
persists it (registry/api/server_routes.py), but cmd_register never
read it out of the config file, so the setting was dropped without any
error. The only way to apply it was a follow-up patch-server call.

The gateway then appended /mcp to upstreams that serve JSON-RPC at

register_service serializes the registration with model_dump, so

drops it, so an unset value still leaves the registry default alone,

fix(nginx): send relative redirects from the front-door server blocks

Since #1501 made the generated location blocks trailing-slash
terminated, a request to a registered MCP server without the trailing
slash hits nginx's automatic "add the slash" 301. absolute_redirect
defaults to on, so nginx rebuilds that Location from the listener that
served the request:

  Location: http://<gateway-host>:8080/registry/<server>/

That is plaintext http:// even though TLS terminates upstream, and the
internal container port, which is not routable from outside the
cluster. Clients follow the redirect and hang until they time out, so
the endpoint only works when the caller happens to include the
trailing slash.

Turn absolute_redirect off in every front-door server block. nginx then
sends a relative Location and the client resolves it against the origin
it dialed, which is correct regardless of how many proxies sit in
front. Set per server block rather than at http scope because the value
that leaks is the listener's own scheme and port.

Signed-off-by: rahul188 <rahulkuchhadia@gmail.com>

fix(nginx): remove duplicate absolute_redirect directive from front-door blocks

#1620 merged an absolute_redirect off; into each front-door server block
that #1635 had already added, leaving two identical directives per block.

fix(nginx,lua): forward caller identity headers in virtual server backend locations

Virtual server backends received no caller identity because:
1. auth_request_set variables ($auth_user, $auth_username) are scoped to
   the parent request and do NOT propagate into ngx.location.capture
   subrequests via proxy_set_header.
2. The /_vs_backend_* internal locations had no mechanism to receive
   identity from the Lua router.

Fix (two-part):
- virtual_router.lua: set X-User and X-Username as request headers
  (ngx.req.set_header) before any ngx.location.capture call. Subrequests
  inherit these headers from the parent.
- nginx_service.py: add proxy_set_header X-User $http_x_user and
  proxy_set_header X-Username $http_x_username to the _vs_backend
  location template so they are forwarded to the upstream MCP server.

This matches the behaviour of direct (non-virtual) server paths, enabling
backends behind virtual servers to enforce write-gates and record audit
attribution.

Tested: Confluence page update through /virtual/development/mcp with
identity correctly resolved by the backend (mcp-atlassian).

fix(lua): fail-closed caller-identity headers on virtual server path

Follow-up to #1627. That PR forwards X-User/X-Username to virtual server
backends via $http_x_user -- a client-controllable request header -- and
the Lua only overwrote it when auth_user was non-empty. A caller with a
userless token (M2M / client-credentials, where $auth_user is empty)
could send a spoofed X-User that survived to the backend, forging the
identity used for write-gates and audit attribution.

Extract the logic into _forward_identity_headers() and make it fail
closed: always set the header from the gateway-validated value, or clear
it when there is no validated user, so a client-supplied value can never
pass through. This matches the direct-server path, which forwards
proxy_set_header X-User $auth_user; unconditionally.

Adds Lua regression tests (tests/lua/test_virtual_router.lua) covering
overwrite-on-validated-user and clear-on-empty/nil-auth_user; the empty
case is red against #1627 and green with this fix.

fix(lua): keep empty inputSchema arrays as [] in virtual tools/list

lua-cjson cannot tell an empty array from an empty object, so any []
that survives a decode/encode round trip comes back as {}. The virtual
router decodes each backend's tools/list response and re-encodes it,
both into the enriched shared-dict cache and into the JSON-RPC result,
so a tool advertising "required": [] reaches the client as "required":
{} and strict MCP clients reject the schema.

_ensure_mcp_schema is the single point every tools/list schema crosses
on all three paths (live enrichment, mapping-file fallback and the
per-request scope filter), so tag empty array-valued keywords there.
Object-valued keywords such as properties are left alone, since {} is
correct for those, and members of properties are not matched against
the keyword list so a tool parameter named "required" is unaffected.

fix(docker): ship OpenResty lua-cjson so virtual router emits [] not {} (#1532)

The virtual_router.lua tools/list aggregation relies on cjson.empty_array_mt
to keep empty JSON-Schema arrays (e.g. "required": []) as [] through the
cjson round trip. That metatable is an OpenResty lua-cjson extension; the
registry image installed Debian lua-cjson 2.1.0, where empty_array_mt is nil,
so the tag was a no-op and empty arrays serialized as {} at runtime (the CI
Lua suite runs in openresty/openresty:alpine, which has the extension, so it
passed while the shipped image did not).

Add a cjson-builder stage that builds OpenResty's lua-cjson against the nginx
lua module's LuaJIT, drop the Debian lua-cjson package, COPY the built cjson.so
into the runtime image, and pin lua_package_cpath so require "cjson" resolves
to it. Fixes the runtime half of #1532; also repairs the pre-existing latent
issue where _as_json_array's empty arrays would render as {} on this runtime.

- tests/lua/test_virtual_router.lua: assert cjson.empty_array_mt is present so
  the suite fails loudly if ever run against a cjson without it.
- tests/integration/test_virtual_empty_schema_e2e.py: live-stack E2E that

fix(keycloak): make the container healthcheck runnable inside the image

The keycloak healthcheck invoked curl, which the Keycloak image deliberately
does not ship (upstream removes HTTP clients to cut attack surface), so the
check could never succeed and the container reported unhealthy forever.

A second, independent fault was stacked on top of it: since Keycloak 25 the
health endpoints moved off the main HTTP port to the management port 9000, so
the probed URL returned 404 even with a working HTTP client. KC_HEALTH_ENABLED
was also absent from docker-compose.yml and docker-compose.prebuilt.yml, which
means /health/ready was not served at all in those deployments.

Replace the check with the bash /dev/tcp redirection documented in the Keycloak
health guide, targeting /health/ready on the management port, and set
KC_HEALTH_ENABLED where it was missing. The status-line match is widened to
HTTP/1.[01] because the server answers an HTTP/1.0 request with its own version.

start_period goes from 60s to 120s so the DB schema migration on first boot no
longer reports the container unhealthy during a normal startup, as requested in
the issue.

The same broken check was present in four other places besides the compose file
named in the report, all running the same image, so they are fixed together:
docker/keycloak/Dockerfile and the ECS task definition in
terraform/aws-ecs/keycloak-ecs.tf.

Add regression tests asserting the invariant across every surface: no curl, the
management port, /health/ready, and KC_HEALTH_ENABLED. All 11 fail against the
pre-fix tree.

A permanently unhealthy container is worse than no healthcheck: it trains
operators to ignore health status and removes the signal for a real outage.

fix(keycloak): pass KEYCLOAK_EXTERNAL_URL to the prebuilt registry, warn when it cannot work

Both the registry and the auth server publish KEYCLOAK_EXTERNAL_URL in their
OAuth discovery documents. When a service does not receive it,
_create_keycloak_provider falls back to KEYCLOAK_URL and the service advertises
the internal Docker DNS name. The response is a well-formed metadata document,
nothing fails server-side, and external MCP clients fail discovery with a
generic OAuth error.

docker-compose.yml was fixed for this in #681; docker-compose.prebuilt.yml was
not, and it is the quick-start path. Add the variable there, and add a compose
parity test covering every discovery-serving service in every compose file so a
third instance of this cannot land silently (see also #1378 for the Podman one).

The silent fallback is the more interesting half of the bug, because it also
covers the case a compose parity test cannot: an operator running a compose file
carried over from an older release. Add a startup diagnostic that names the
problem instead of leaving it to be inferred from a client-side error:

  - KEYCLOAK_EXTERNAL_URL unset               -> WARNING
  - single-label host (container DNS name)    -> WARNING
  - private, link-local or reserved address   -> WARNING
  - loopback                                  -> INFO
  - globally routable                         -> silent

Loopback is deliberately INFO rather than WARNING: it is the shipped default for
local development and genuinely works for a client on the same host, so warning
on it would fire on every default deployment and train operators to ignore the
line, which is the failure mode this is meant to prevent.

Note that RFC 5737 documentation ranges (203.0.113.0/24 and friends) are
is_private on Python 3.12.4+, so they warn too. That is correct, and the tests
pin it so a future reader does not "fix" it.

The nginx upstream in registry/core/nginx_service.py is deliberately left on
KEYCLOAK_URL: that hop is container-to-container and must stay internal.

fix(servers): reject a half-filled provider pair with 400 instead of 500

provider_organization and provider_url are only meaningful as a pair. Both form
handlers guarded on `or`, so a half-filled pair entered the branch and built
AgentProvider with one field set to None. AgentProvider requires both, per the
A2A specification quoted in its own docstring, so Pydantic raised a
ValidationError that no handler catches and the caller got a 500 with nothing
indicating which field was at fault.

The pair has a second, quieter failure mode the report did not cover: an HTML
form submits an empty string for a field the user left alone, not None, and
AgentProvider(organization="", url="https://...") passes Pydantic because str
has no minimum length. So the same half-filled pair produced either an unhandled
500 or a stored provider with an empty field, depending on whether the frontend
omitted the blank field or submitted it.

Replace the inline construction at both call sites with one _build_provider_entry
helper that treats None, empty and whitespace-only alike as absent:

  - neither field     -> no provider; the pair stays optional as a whole
  - exactly one field -> 400 naming the missing field
  - both fields       -> provider built, values stripped

Note that changing `or` to `and` would have fixed the 500 while silently
discarding a half-filled pair. This rejects it instead.

The issue suggested expressing the constraint on the request model. That does
not apply directly: both handlers take Annotated[str | None, Form()] parameters,
not a model. A shared helper gives the same one-rule-instead-of-three and keeps
the 400 at the layer that can name the field. The JSON PUT path takes a Pydantic
body with provider: AgentProvider, so FastAPI already returns 422 there; it is
unchanged.

One test asserts the exception type rather than only the status code: a
half-filled pair must raise HTTPException and never reach Pydantic. An uncaught
ValidationError is what produced the 500, so pinning the type stops a refactor
from reintroducing it while still returning 400 on some other path.

fix(auth): filter tools/list against the normalized server name

The tools/list response filter was given the proxy path (e.g. "myserver/mcp")
while the access check earlier in the same request used the registered name
("myserver"), stripped via _registered_server_from_proxy_path in
_authorize_forwarded_mcp_body. A scope document keyed on the registered name
matched nothing under the suffixed key, so every tool was removed.

The failure mode is worse than the bug. The client gets a valid JSON-RPC
response with an empty tools array: not an error, so nothing surfaces. The
connector looks healthy, the server is listed, and it has no tools. The only
signal was the filter's own before/after counts in the auth-server log.

Strip the transport suffix at the call site, matching what the access check in
the same request already did, and document the contract on
filter_tools_list_response so a future caller holding a proxy path does not
reintroduce it.

Two diagnostics, because the reporter is right that the failure mode is worse
than the defect:

  - Log which scope entry matched. before/after counts alone cannot tell a
    correct filter from a scope-key mismatch; scopes_matched can.
  - When a server has no server_access entry in ANY of the caller's scopes and
    all tools were dropped, log ERROR with remediation. That is a configuration
    error, not an empty allowlist, and the two are indistinguishable in the
    response.

The empty result still stays empty: authorization continues to fail closed, and
the response shape is unchanged, so no client sees different behaviour. Only the
log output differs. The diagnostic uses get_server_scopes_bulk, so it costs one
round-trip regardless of scope count, against the N*M per-tool lookups the
filter already issues.

The diagnostic is fully guarded: filter_tools_list_response documents "never
raises", so a scope-store failure or an unexpected shape must not turn a
successful tools/list into a 500. A test pins that.

_patch_scope_repo_allow_all now also stubs get_server_scopes_bulk. Without it
the diagnostic would receive a bare AsyncMock and the shared helper would let
tests pass for the wrong reason.
