feat(gateway-proxy): foundation — SSRF egress guard, ProxyableMixin, config

First slice of the "proxy any registry entity through the gateway" feature.
Pure scaffolding: not wired into request handling, and every toggle ships
disabled/fail-closed, so this is a no-op in production.

- registry/utils/ip_guard.py (new): the single canonical SSRF IP classifier.
  Recognizes obfuscated IPv4 literal spellings (decimal/octal/hex/short-form/
  trailing-dot, matching inet_aton) and unwraps every IPv6 transport that embeds
  an IPv4 address (IPv4-mapped, NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, 6to4 2002::/16, Teredo
  2001::/32) before category-checking. Always denies link-local (cloud metadata),
  unspecified, reserved, and multicast; allow_private relaxes ONLY loopback /
  private-unicast / CGNAT / ULA. Branch order is deliberate so multi-category
  addresses (e.g. ::1 is loopback+reserved, 240.0.0.1 is reserved+private)
  classify correctly.
- registry/schemas/proxy_mixin.py (new): ProxyableMixin (is_proxied,
  proxy_target_url + refresh bookkeeping fields), a Pydantic field_validator that
  runs the egress guard at the model edge, and resolve_proxy_target(). The guard
  is a static check (no DNS); the authoritative rebind defense is the network
  egress policy, documented as such. resolve_proxy_target returns the stored
  target verbatim — callers that build a live route MUST re-run the guard (the
  render/persist enforcement hooks land in later slices).
- registry/core/config.py: four registry-consumed gateway settings, all
  fail-closed (generic-proxy + canonical-namespace disabled, allow-private off),
  plus a strict nginx size-token validator on the client-body-size string
  (rendered verbatim into nginx, so it's a config-injection surface).
- Consolidate the two existing hand-rolled SSRF guards onto ip_guard:
  ard_net_guard._is_blocked_ip and skill_service._is_private_ip now delegate to
  it, which closes a shared NAT64/6to4/Teredo blind spot in the ARD-ingestion and
  skill-fetch paths (their existing tests still pass; new embedded-transport and
  CGNAT cases added).
- custom_entity_models: reverse the "never proxied" docstring — custom entities
  are a first-class proxy target.

Tests: exhaustive ip_guard vector coverage (every metadata spelling + all four
IPv6 wrappers + allow_private blast-radius + CGNAT-assumption pin), model-edge
validation, and the migrated guards. 251 tests pass across the affected suites.

feat(gateway-proxy): wire ProxyableMixin into entity models + service layer

Makes the is_proxied/proxy_target_url opt-in real end-to-end for the new
generic-proxy targets (skill, agent, custom entity), while keeping the feature
disabled by default and enforcing the security invariants at the right layers.

Models:
- ProxyableMixin on the 5 storage models (ServerInfo, AgentCard, SkillCard,
  CustomEntityRecord) + the request/patch models (ServiceRegistrationRequest,
  AgentRegistrationRequest, AgentCardPatch, SkillRegistrationRequest,
  CustomEntityCreate/Update, ServerUpdateRequest, ServerCardPatch). Virtual

- Read-safe storage vs. fail-fast edge (the load-bearing split): storage models
  NEVER raise on a stored proxy_target_url (they are reconstructed from the DB on
  every read; raising would vanish a bypass-written record from every listing).
  The SSRF egress raise and the target-required raise live on the request/patch
  models (API edge, no vanish risk) via egress_guard_validator and a non-read-safe

feat(gateway-proxy): federation isolation — proxy config never crosses the boundary

Owner decision: no proxying federated entities, either direction. A synced-in

- strip_proxy_fields / PROXY_FIELD_NAMES in proxy_mixin: removes the 5 proxy_*

- INGEST: strip on every peer-content write — peer sync (_store_synced_servers/

Adds the projected, indexed query the nginx-render hot path will use to collect

feat(gateway-proxy): generic-proxy internal token (mint + verify)

Adds the short-lived HS256 token for the generic reverse-proxy hop
(/proxy/{entity_type}/{entity_path}), modeled on the mcp-proxy token. Groundwork
— no hop consumes it yet; feature ships disabled.

- GENERIC_PROXY_AUDIENCE / TOKEN_USE, distinct from every other internal
  audience (mcp-proxy, mcp-registry-ui, mcp-registry service), so PyJWT's
  verify_aud makes cross-hop replay impossible in either direction.
- mint_generic_proxy_token binds TWO claims: entity_type AND the FULL registered
  path (not just the first segment, since registered paths are multi-segment).
  upstream_url is required and pinned from the token, never headers.
- verify_generic_proxy_token: fail-closed parity with verify_mcp_proxy_token,
  plus a stronger guard — rejects cross-type replay (entity_type must match),
  binds the full path on a SEGMENT boundary (skills/proxy-demo does NOT authorize
  skills/proxy-demo-evil), allows a sub-path strictly under the bound entity, and
  rejects '..' segments. Reads X-Internal-Token-Generic (distinct header per hop).
- GENERIC_PROXY_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS knob (falls back to INTERNAL_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS,
  same floor) via a new optional ttl_seconds param on _mint_internal_token —
  no behavior change for the mcp-proxy / registry-UI tokens.
- Hardening: _mint_internal_token now merges extra_claims
  FIRST then base claims, so a reserved key (aud/exp/iss) in extra_claims can
  never override the base — structural, not convention. Docstring records the

refactor(ssrf): converge the generic-proxy egress guard onto url_guard's pinned transport

The generic proxy had its own SSRF path (proxy_mixin + ip_guard, blanket
allow_private bool) while the rest of the repo used the canonical url_guard
(pinned httpx transport, per-host/CIDR allowlist). Worse, the generic hop fetched
with a BARE httpx.AsyncClient — no connect-time IP pinning — violating the
CLAUDE.md invariant. Converge them into one guard.

- ip_guard becomes the single IP classifier. ip_denial_reason gains a two-tier
  allowlist: an explicit metadata set (169.254.169.254 AND the IPv6 fd00:ec2::254)
  checked FIRST and never overridable — fixing a real gap where fd00:ec2::254 is
  unique-local (is_private) and allow_private would have reached it; an
  allowed_cidrs param that re-permits any non-metadata category; and the coarse
  allow_private bool that relaxes only loopback/private/CGNAT.
- url_guard._is_blocked_ip delegates to ip_guard (deletes its weaker inline
  classifier + duplicated metadata/CGNAT constants). validate_url and the pinned
  transport parse literals via coerce_ip_literal, so obfuscated spellings
  (hex/octal/decimal/embedded-v4) are caught for skills/federation/agents too.
  PROXY_PROFILE honors gateway_proxy_allow_private_targets.
- The generic hop (buffered + streaming) now uses
  guarded_async_client(profile=PROXY_PROFILE, verify=...) — connect-to-pinned-IP +
  per-target TLS, re-validated per redirect. A fetch-time egress block is caught
  and returned as a sanitized 502 (never leaking the target), not an opaque 500.
- proxy_mixin's egress functions become thin PROXY_PROFILE adapters over
  url_guard.validate_url, translating UrlValidationError -> EgressPolicyError (a
  ValueError, preserving the Pydantic 4xx). Registration and fetch now share one
  classifier + allowlist. resolve_and_validate runs the sync guard in a worker
  thread so DNS can't block the event loop.

Behavior notes: scheme errors and empty-host now raise EgressPolicyError (still
ValueError -> 4xx; no consumer caught EgressPolicyError specifically). An operator
CIDR can re-permit link-local/reserved/multicast (a precise, intentional
statement) but never the metadata IP. A hostname allowlist (ssrf_allowed_hosts /
github_extra_hosts) still bypasses IP validation for that host by design — the
metadata guarantee covers literal + resolved-IP targets, documented on the guard.

feat(egress): application-layer encryption for per-user egress credentials (#1665)

Encrypt per-user egress credentials with AES-256-GCM before they are handed to
the secret-store backend (AWS Secrets Manager / OpenBao), so the vault holds a
versioned ciphertext envelope instead of usable PAT / OAuth access / refresh
tokens. Gated by a new dedicated root key, EGRESS_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;
empty preserves the legacy plaintext behavior.

Crypto (registry/secrets/credential_codec.py):
- Per-(auth_method, user_id) key derived from the root key via HKDF-SHA256 (the
  root key is never used directly), keyed on the same canonical principal that
  namespaces the vault.
- AEAD associated data binds the full (auth_method, user_id, provider,
  server_path) address AND the envelope version/algorithm/key_id, so a
  ciphertext copied to another user/server/provider fails authentication and the
  metadata cannot be tampered to steer decryption.
- Fresh random 96-bit nonce per write; versioned envelope
  {_encrypted, version, algorithm, key_id, nonce, ciphertext}.

Fail-closed: an envelope seen without a key, a wrong key, tamper, unsupported
version/algorithm/key_id, or malformed payload all raise; credentials are never
returned or re-persisted as plaintext, and no plaintext/key material is logged.

Backward compatibility / migration:
- Both backends encode on write and decode on read; reads recognize legacy
  plaintext and the new envelope.
- Legacy plaintext entries are transparently re-encrypted on first read
  (read-repair), non-blocking, using compare-and-set so a migration never
  clobbers a concurrent token refresh: Secrets Manager under the principal
  mutation lease, OpenBao via KV v2 cas.
- EGRESS_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_REQUIRE_ENCRYPTED (strict mode) rejects any
  lingering plaintext once migration is complete.

Key custody & rotation: the root key must live outside the secret-store trust
boundary it protects. Rotation is a destructive cutover today (single active
key); the envelope carries a key_id as the seam for a future multi-key keyring.

Deployment surfaces wired for the key: docker-compose (x3), Helm registry chart
(secret), Terraform ECS (Secrets Manager valueFrom + IAM). CDK left untouched
(it has no egress vars yet). Docs and .env.example updated.

fix(auth): strip ingress proxy-context headers on the egress hop

_forward_headers() copies incoming request headers to the upstream MCP
server, stripping hop-by-hop headers and client auth. It did not strip
proxy-context headers (X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Host,
X-Forwarded-Port, X-Forwarded-Prefix, Forwarded, X-Original-URI,
X-Original-URL), so a stale ingress scheme or host set by the front-end
TLS-terminating proxy is relayed onto the separate Gateway to upstream
hop. An upstream that trusts these headers can see, for example,
X-Forwarded-Proto: http on a connection that is actually HTTPS and
issue an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, producing a redirect loop through the
gateway.

Add _PROXY_CONTEXT_HEADERS and strip it in _forward_headers, keeping
X-Forwarded-For untouched since some deployments rely on it to see the
real client IP upstream.

Fixes #1625

fix(keycloak): rewrite every internal URL in the discovery document

authorization_server_metadata rewrote the internal Keycloak URL onto the
external host for ten named fields. Everything it did not enumerate kept the
internal Docker URL, and the nested mtls_endpoint_aliases object was not walked
at all, so every key inside it leaked:

  check_session_iframe
  backchannel_authentication_endpoint
  pushed_authorization_request_endpoint
  mtls_endpoint_aliases.* (all eight)

The primary endpoints (issuer, authorization, token, jwks, registration) were
correct, so the document looks right at a glance. A client using PAR, CIBA,
mTLS client auth or OIDC session management is handed an unreachable internal
host and fails in a way that is hard to attribute to discovery. An allowlist
also means every field a future Keycloak release adds starts out broken.

Walk the whole document instead. A value is rewritten because it points at the
internal host, not because someone remembered to list its field name, so new
fields and nested objects are covered without maintenance.

Two things fall out of doing it properly:

  - Anchor the match at a URL boundary. The old code used a bare startswith, so
    an internal base of "http://keycloak:8080" also matched
    "http://keycloak:80801" -- a different port on the same host -- and rewrote
    it. Only "/", "?", "#" or end-of-string now count as a boundary.

  - Build new containers rather than mutating in place.
    _get_openid_configuration is lru_cached, so rewriting a nested dict in place
    would poison the cache for every later caller, including the internal-URL
    consumers that must keep pointing at the cluster host. A test pins this.

Ten tests, of which the primary one asserts the invariant over the whole
document rather than named fields: no string anywhere in the result may contain
the internal URL. Six fail against the pre-fix tree.

Reported by us in #1649 after the compose fix landed; that issue stayed open
because passing the variable to the registry was only half of it.

Refs #1649

fix(security): fail closed when failed-scan auto-disable cannot disable a server

Follow-up to #1697. That PR moved the failed-scan auto-disable in the operator
scripts from the internal SECRET_KEY route to the user-authenticated
POST /api/servers/toggle. The old internal route had no per-user check, so the
disable always succeeded; the new route requires the gateway token to hold
toggle_service on the just-registered server. When the token is missing,
expired, or lacks that permission, the toggle returns non-200 and the block
only logged the error, leaving a server that FAILED its security scan enabled
and reachable (fail-open).

scripts stay byte-identical in the edited block.

  registers, or the safety net is a no-op.

  EGRESS_REGISTRY_INTERNAL_URL at the internal listener (registry:8091, the #1655

feat(url-guard): allow operator-named trusted IdP hosts for egress OAuth

The credentialed-OAuth SSRF profile requires every egress OAuth token
endpoint to resolve to a public address, behind an allowlist that is
hardcoded empty and reads no settings. A self-hosted IdP legitimately
resolves to a private address, so per-user egress consent against an
internal Keycloak (or Entra behind Private Link) fails with
"token endpoint blocked by security policy" and no setting can relax it.

This is arguably inconsistent: the gateway is already required to make
credentialed calls to that same IdP for its own authentication, via
KEYCLOAK_URL and KEYCLOAK_CA_BUNDLE. Unlike a federation peer or a
registrant-supplied proxy target, the IdP is operator-configured
infrastructure, not attacker-influenced input.

Add EGRESS_OAUTH_TRUSTED_IDP_HOSTS, following the existing
_skill_allowlist / _proxy_allowlist pattern, and keep it deliberately
narrower than both:

- hosts only, matched exactly: no CIDRs and no wildcards, so each IdP
  must be named in full
- its own dedicated setting: it does NOT read ssrf_allowed_hosts,
  ssrf_allowed_cidrs or github_extra_hosts, so the "must not inherit any
  operator proxy/skill bypass" invariant in the docstring still holds and
  an entry there still cannot re-permit a token endpoint
- require_https stays on, and the hard-denied categories (cloud/workload
  credential, metadata, link-local, reserved, multicast) are unchanged
  because they are evaluated before the hostname relaxation
- defaults to empty, so existing deployments are unaffected

Tests cover the private-IdP happy path, exact-match-only (no subdomain or
parent inference), HTTPS still enforced, transport pinning to the resolved
IP, the metadata endpoint staying denied for an allowlisted host, and both
the proxy and skill allowlists still being unable to relax a token target.

  Error: creating VPC Security Group Rule
    with module.mcp_gateway.module.ecs_service_registry

  api error InvalidParameterValue: Invalid rule description.

the gateway generic proxy. Existing deployments that already hold the rule
were unaffected, which is why it went unnoticed.

beside the RESERVED_CUSTOM_HEADER_NAMES denylist it carves out of, and have all
three read it. Every other reserved name stays refused at every layer.

test(gateway-proxy): add operator test clients, preflight gate, and regression suite

The generic reverse proxy's two headline capabilities -- response streaming and
static upstream auth headers -- cannot be exercised by pytest: both need a live
stack and a real backend credential. Neither had any coverage, so a buffered
response or a silently dropped credential would pass a 200-only check.

Four scripts under tests/scripts/, none of them pytest tests:

- gateway_test_support.py -- everything that is about the GATEWAY rather than a
  particular upstream: the credential split, entity discovery, the per-verb
  scope check, and status interpretation. Shared so the clients cannot drift.
- openai_gateway_client.py -- modes models (GET authz), chat (POST authz plus
  the CSRF bearer exemption), and stream (SSE).
- bedrock_gateway_client.py -- converse and the AWS event-stream path, whose
  length-prefixed binary frames are why curl -N shows no data: lines.
- verify_caller_creds.py -- proves a caller-supplied key is the credential that
  reaches the backend, and that the gateway stores none.

The streaming assertions make a buffered response fail loudly instead of passing
on a 200: each stream mode records time-to-first-chunk, chunk count, and the
largest inter-chunk gap, and fails on one chunk or on every chunk arriving at the
same instant.

verify_caller_creds.py needs two calls because a 200 alone cannot attribute a
credential -- a stored operator default produces the same 200. The 401 with no
caller key is the load-bearing half: nothing stored means nothing to inject.

gateway-proxy-preflight.sh gates the suite. It checks every credential file,
decodes the gateway JWT and rejects an expired one, checks the .env settings and
/health, and exits non-zero on the first missing prerequisite, so a missing key
fails on the spot instead of surfacing later as what looks like a proxy bug.

gateway-proxy-regression.md is the manual suite the scripts serve. It records
two findings that cost real time. Against a CloudFront-fronted deployment every
curl needs --compressed, because CloudFront gzips JSON and curl does not
decompress unless asked, so a working call prints unreadable bytes while
-w '%{http_code}' reports 200. And demoting a stored operator default to a
caller-only slot takes two rotations, because omitting a value means keep --
the write-only convention the UI editor depends on.

Error paths name their cause rather than raising: a gateway JWT is only valid
for the deployment whose auth-server signed it, since iss and aud are identical
across deployments while each signs with its own SECRET_KEY, and that 401 reads
like a scope problem otherwise.

feat(gateway-proxy): connect affordance, operator notes, and a CLI create path

Three gaps for anyone using the generic proxy: a caller could not discover the
URL to call, an operator had nowhere to record how to call it, and registering a
proxied record meant hand-writing JSON.

Connect affordance
------------------
ProxyConnectButton opens a popover with the full client-facing URL, the backend
it forwards to, the operator's notes, and a copy button. It is wired into the
custom-entity card and detail modal and the skill card.

The control always renders, disabled when the entity is not proxied, so its
absence never has to be interpreted -- a missing button is indistinguishable
from a bug. Presence of proxy_client_url is the single source of truth for "is
this reachable through the gateway": the server derives it only for a proxied
entity, so no separate is_proxied prop can drift out of sync with it.

The URL is selectable text plus copy, never a live link, because a caller must
append their own API sub-path and send auth headers -- the base URL is not
navigable on its own. gatewayClientUrl centralises the trailing slash, which
matters because the nginx location ends in one, so the bare path answers 301 and
a POST would be silently downgraded to GET.

ProxyField's label becomes an action rather than a state readout: it previously
said "Proxied" / "Not proxied" next to the toggle that already showed that.

proxy_connect_notes
-------------------
Optional operator free text on a proxied entity, capped at 2000 characters,
never interpreted by the gateway. It answers the question a client URL alone
cannot: which sub-path to append and what the request looks like.

Patch semantics follow proxy_target_url -- None means leave unchanged, so an
empty string is the only way to clear notes. Both directions are tested because
a reader cannot tell them apart from the field declaration.

The field joins PROXY_FIELD_NAMES, so federation strips it in both directions:
notes describe a local backend, so a peer must not receive ours and must not
plant its own.

CLI
---
custom-proxy-create builds the proxy fields from flags instead of a JSON
record: --target-url, --streaming, --auth-passthrough for a caller-overridable
Authorization slot, and --connect-notes. --registry-url and --token-file now
default to http://localhost and .token.

Verification
------------
The popover was verified in a real browser with the app stylesheet loaded, since
without it the Tailwind positioning classes are inert and a visual check proves
nothing: position absolute, z-index 20, inside the viewport, and at the 2000
character maximum the notes block clips to its max height and scrolls while the
dialog stays bounded. Escape closes, an outside mousedown closes, a disabled
trigger does nothing, and copy places the trailing-slash URL on the clipboard.
Dark mode renders with readable contrast.

Backend coverage is at the route boundary as well as the service, because an
older build accepts a request carrying proxy_connect_notes and silently drops it
as an unknown key -- the call looks like a success while the notes never arrive.
That is exactly what a live create against a deployment without this change
does, so the route test is what would have caught it. Every new test was
confirmed to fail with the source change removed.

fix(scopes): grant registry-admins HTTP verbs on gateway-proxied entities

An administrator was denied every gateway-proxied route on a fresh install.

The generic proxy authorizes by HTTP verb, and the resolver splits the value
spaces on purpose: for an HTTP verb the legacy "all"/"*" wildcard does NOT grant
(_HTTP_VERB_WILDCARD in auth_server/server.py:1961-1970). The guard is right --
it stops an entity flipped to is_proxied from silently turning an existing MCP
wildcard into DELETE/PUT authority. The gap is that the shipped admin seed only
carries methods:["all"], so admins hold the MCP wildcard and no HTTP verb at all.

The symptom is a 403 that reads like a routing or registration failure rather
than a missing grant, and it cannot be repaired through the management API: it
refuses wildcard server_access entries ("Wildcards must be seeded server-side"),
and a read-modify-write of this group fails separately. scripts/registry-admins.json
is loaded straight into mcp_scopes_default by scripts/init-documentdb-indexes.py,
so the seed is the only path.

Observed live: GET through a proxied entity returned 403 with the group holding
methods:["all"]; after pushing exactly this rule into the collection, the OpenAI
and Bedrock proxy suites passed end to end.

Scope of the grant: registry-admins already holds every MCP method and tool on
every server plus full agent actions, so HTTP verbs on proxied entities add no
authority it could not already reach by editing the entity. The value-space split
keeps protecting every OTHER group, which is what it was written for -- a
non-admin group's MCP wildcard still grants no HTTP verb.

Tests drive the real resolver with the on-disk seed rather than asserting the
file's shape, so they keep holding if the wildcard token or the split is
reworked. Both were confirmed to fail against the state they guard: removing the
rule fails the five verb cases, and relaxing the split so "all" also grants HTTP
verbs fails the escalation test.

The HTTP-verb coverage lives in tests/auth_server/unit/ rather than beside the
other seed assertions in tests/security/, because importing auth_server.server
needs the auth-server path setup only that suite provides.

fix(a2a): build the agent-card route from the URL origin, not the JSON-RPC endpoint

Closes #1724

Every spec-following A2A agent registered with a path in its URL had a broken
agent-card route through the gateway. The route appended the well-known suffix to
the registered URL, but the A2A spec puts the card document at a well-known path
on the ORIGIN and lets the card's own "url" field name the endpoint anywhere. For
an agent registered as https://host/a2a the gateway asked for
https://host/a2a/.well-known/agent-card.json and got a 404.

Reverse-proxy routing itself was fine; only the card path was wrong. On the
registry where this was found, 94 of 122 live agents were affected and none could
serve a card through the gateway.

Two sites had the same defect. The second was found while verifying the first:

- registry/core/nginx_service.py: the generated card location's proxy_pass now
  targets scheme://netloc. The block already parsed the URL for the Host header,
  so this reuses what was in scope.
- registry/utils/agent_validator.py: the registration-time reachability probe
  fetched {url}/.well-known/agent-card.json, so it reported a spec-following
  agent unreachable for the same reason.

_build_agent_health_urls in registry/api/agent_routes.py already derived the card
from the origin, so three call sites disagreed and only one matched the spec.
That is why the health check reported these agents healthy while their gateway
card route 404ed. All three now agree.

Not a data problem: the agent is right, the registry stored the card's url
verbatim, and no code inserts the path. No record is modified and no migration is
needed. A path-less URL made the bug invisible, because appending to the url and
to the origin produce the same string.

The JSON-RPC route still appends the registered path, which is correct there.

Verified against a live spec-compliant agent on a rebuilt stack. Before, the
rendered route read .../a2a/.well-known/agent-card.json and 404ed; after, it
targets the origin and returns 200 application/json whose "url" has been
rewritten to the gateway by agent_card_rewrite.lua -- which it can only do on a
card body it actually parsed. The JSON-RPC route stayed byte-identical to a
direct backend POST, the path-less agent's route is unchanged, and all 8 rendered
card routes on that stack target an origin with none nesting a path.

Unit tests cover a path suffix, a multi-segment path, a port, the path-less
regression guard, the JSON-RPC route keeping its path, and the card route
retaining its X-Authorization and Cookie strips (the #1391 egress trust model).
The three path-carrying cases and one validator case were confirmed to fail
without the source change.

docs(gateway-proxy): add the operational guide, and fix a log string nothing emitted

The generic proxy had a design doc and no operating instructions: nothing that
said how to turn it on, register a route, choose a credential model, or read a
failure. This adds the guide, links it from the README and the docs index, and
corrects the design doc's client-path section.

The guide is organised around the four credential models -- keyless, fixed
operator header, caller passthrough, per-user vault -- because who owns the
credential is the decision everything else follows from, then works through four
patterns: model inference, generic REST, skills and documents, and A2A agents.

Corrected while verifying, not written from the design intent:

- The design doc described the client-facing location as `/{entity_type}/{path}`.
  It is `/{prefix}/{entity_type}/{name}` with the leading namespace segment
  stripped and a trailing slash, per build_proxy_client_path
  (registry/schemas/proxy_mixin.py:499). A skill at /skills/pdf is served at
  /gateway/skill/pdf/.

- `generic-proxy feature DISABLED` appeared in the guide, the regression suite,
  and the preflight gate. No code emits it. The real line is `Generic proxy
  egress self-check FAILED`, with `Generic proxy egress self-check PASSED;
  feature active` as its healthy counterpart. In the preflight gate this was a
  live defect, not a typo: the grep matched nothing, so the check always reported
  ok and a latched-off feature reached the suite as an unexplained 404.

Two traps documented because both cost real time and neither is visible locally:

- Behind a gzipping edge, curl needs --compressed. Without it a working call
  prints unreadable bytes while -w '%{http_code}' still reports 200. The Quick
  start examples now carry the flag so they are correct against either endpoint.

- A route registered seconds ago has no nginx location yet, so the request falls
  through to the frontend shell and returns 200 text/html. A status-only check
  reports success. The Quick start now prints the content type, and the
  troubleshooting entry names registration timing as a cause.

Every claim was checked against the source rather than the design: all four
cited metrics and all three log phrases exist, every internal link and cited
file path resolves, and each documented CLI subcommand is real per argparse.
The Quick start was run verbatim against a live deployment -- it returned

feat(metrics): classify gateway-proxy routes and put the authz key in the server label

Part 1 of #1735. The hop's own outcome counter follows in part 2.

Gateway-proxied requests all classified as target_kind="unknown", because
_TARGET_KIND_RULES has no rule for them, and carried server="gateway" -- the
first URL path segment captured as though it were a server name. On a live stack
that put 40 gateway calls in one indistinguishable bucket, and the traffic was
separable only by accident: changing GATEWAY_PROXY_PREFIX would have removed even
that.

Classification now reads the X-Generic-Proxy-Kind marker nginx sets on each
generated location, yielding generic_proxy_skill, generic_proxy_agent, or
generic_proxy_custom. It does NOT key on GATEWAY_PROXY_PREFIX: docker-compose
passes that variable to the registry container only, and auth_server/ has zero
references to it, so a prefix-keyed rule would have kept filing gateway traffic
as unknown for any non-default prefix while in-process tests passed. Operators
define custom types at will, so every non-skill, non-agent type collapses to
generic_proxy_custom and the label set stays at three values.

The server label now carries the entity's authz key, built from
X-Generic-Proxy-Kind and X-Entity-Path with the same expression /validate uses at
server.py:3955. A 403 in the metric therefore names the exact string to put in a
scope rule. Deriving the key from the client path would not work:
build_proxy_client_path strips the registered path's leading namespace segment,
so a skill at /skills/pdf renders as /gateway/skill/pdf and yields "skill/pdf"
while the real key is "skill/skills/pdf" -- a rule that cannot exist.

The label also now routes through the shared LabelCardinalityLimiter, which it
previously bypassed on the stated grounds that it was "derived from the
registry-controlled URI path". That premise no longer holds. X-Original-URL is
$request_uri and the generated gateway location is a trailing-slash prefix match,
so every segment past the registered prefix is caller-chosen; custom records are
also UUID-keyed, so create-and-delete churn would mint a series per cycle. The
comment stating the old premise is corrected.

server stays OFF the duration histogram
---------------------------------------
One attribute dict fed both instruments. The histogram carries 16 le buckets plus
_count and _sum, so a per-entity server label costs 19 series per
(success, method) combination instead of 1 -- about 3,800 series and 444 MB at 100

docs: the shared operator key is optional and for service-to-service only

Both the README highlight and the FAQ offered "each caller brings their own key
or share one operator key" as an even choice. It is not one. Caller passthrough
is the default and the only model that keeps provider quota, rate limits, and
billing attributable to the person who made the call. A shared key pools all of
that, so one user's runaway loop throttles everybody, and per-user attribution at
the provider disappears -- the registry audit log still names the caller, but the
provider cannot. It earns its place for a batch job, a scheduled pipeline, or an
agent running under a machine identity, and nowhere near a user-facing path.

The FAQ also stated the operator-key option more loosely than the code allows.
validate_custom_headers permits `Authorization` only as a caller-OVERRIDABLE slot
(credential_encryption.py:130-134): it may carry an operator default that any
caller who sends their own key overrides, and a fixed, non-overridable
`Authorization` is refused at registration because operator-owned bearers belong
in the egress vault. Since OpenAI and Bedrock both read `Authorization`, a reader
following the old wording would have registered something the registry rejects.
Providers that read a different header, such as Azure OpenAI's `api-key`, can
hold a fixed operator value, so the article now says which case is which.

fix(skills): detect redirects from history, not the pinned-IP URL

The guarded transport pins every request to a validated IP by rewriting
the URL host, keeping identity in the Host header and TLS SNI. That makes
response.url differ from the requested URL on every fetch and read as an
IP literal.

skill_service treated that difference as evidence of a redirect, so a
SKILL.md on a forge whose hostname is allowlisted via GITHUB_EXTRA_HOSTS
but resolves to a private address was refused with "Redirect to unsafe
URL blocked", naming an address the caller never typed. Registration and
parsing returned 400, the health check reported unhealthy, and the
content endpoint raised an SSRF error. The check shipped in 1.23.0 and
was harmless until the pinning rewrite landed in 1.29.0.

_unsafe_redirect_target reads response.history instead. No history means
no redirect, so nothing is judged. Each real hop is validated under the
identity the transport preserved rather than the address it dialled.

Redirects to a metadata IP or to a private host that is not allowlisted
stay refused, and the transport's own per-hop validation is unchanged.
Two of the eight tests cover those negatives and pass before the fix;
the other six fail without it.

fix(dedup): calibrate the threshold against real indexed documents (0.6 -> 0.45)

Executing the test plan against a live registry showed 0.6 was measured on the
wrong thing. The design calibrated it on symmetric stripped strings, but the
deployed comparison is asymmetric: the query is stripped while each candidate is
compared on its *indexed* text, which keeps its boilerplate and also carries
`Tags: ...` and flattened metadata. That dilution costs roughly 0.2 of cosine.

Measured on a live 404-document index with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, stripped query vs
the actual indexed text:

  two entries with identical name and description   0.6042
  genuine near-duplicate (topic extractor)          0.8024
  genuine near-duplicate (meeting topic miner)      0.5371
  genuine near-duplicate (weather radar/forecast)   0.5104
  unrelated (topic vs category)                     0.1652
  unrelated (topic vs payroll)                      0.0645
  unrelated (topic vs weather)                      0.0005

At 0.6 an exact content duplicate passed by 0.004 and two genuine
near-duplicates were missed. Adding two more tags to a server would have pushed
the exact duplicate under the gate. Unrelated pairs top out at 0.25, so 0.45
sits in the middle of an empty band and catches all three genuine cases.

Verified at 0.45 against the same live registry, including its 149 real

moves these pairs by at most +0.06 (0.6042 -> 0.6642), because the dilution
comes from tags and metadata rather than from boilerplate tokens. It would cost
a full corpus re-index for no useful separation.

fix(terraform): make the dedup threshold validation null-safe

`terraform apply` failed on the new null default:

    Error: Operation failed
      on variables.tf line 399, in variable "dedup_score_threshold":
        condition = var.dedup_score_threshold == null || (var.dedup_score_threshold >= 0 && ...)
      var.dedup_score_threshold is null
      Error during operation: argument must not be null.

HCL's `||` does not short-circuit: the right operand is evaluated even when the
left is already true, so the range comparison ran against null and raised. Use
coalesce, which is null-safe and reads plainly.

renders "" for the task-definition env, an explicit 0.85 passes and renders,
and 1.5 is still rejected with the range error.

feat(cli): add check-duplicates and pre-flight it before registering

Until now the duplicate check had exactly one caller: the registration UI.
`registry_management.py` never consulted it and neither does `POST /register`,
so a CLI or CI registration learned about a duplicate only from the 409 that
followed — and only when the path collided. A duplicate that reused an existing
backend URL under a new path registered silently.

Concretely, `cli/examples/cloudflare-docs-server-config.json` describes a server
already present in a live registry. Registering it returned 409 with no
indication of what it duplicated. Now:

    $ registry_management.py check-duplicates --config cloudflare-docs-server-config.json
    WARNING server 'Cloudflare Documentation MCP Server' collides with 1 existing entity
            on the same URL:
    WARNING   /cloudflare-docs (mcp_server) - Cloudflare Documentation MCP Server
              [exact URL match]

`check-duplicates` takes either a registration config (`--config`, read exactly
as the register commands read it) or explicit `--name/--description/--url`,
across `--type server|agent|skill`, with `--json` for machine use.

`register`, `agent-register`, and `skill-register` now pre-flight the check and
report what they find. They still register: the feature is advisory and the
server does not gate on it, so neither does the CLI. `--fail-on-duplicate` turns
it into a CI gate that aborts before the API call, and `--skip-duplicate-check`
opts out. A check that cannot run is logged and ignored — a hint must never be
the reason a registration fails.

Also fixes the client's content-type routing: `/api/servers/check-duplicates`
would have been sent form-encoded, since only PUT/PATCH under `/api/servers/`
were routed as JSON.

Verified against a live registry: the collision above, an agent similarity hit
at 0.9148, `--fail-on-duplicate` exiting 1 with zero API calls made, and
`--skip-duplicate-check` bypassing the check entirely. 22 new unit tests.

feat(observability): report the auth-path traffic mix per deployment and across the fleet

Every /validate call already recorded which auth path it took, as the
`method` label on mcpgw_registry_auth_request_total. Three things stopped
that from being useful, and this fixes all three.

A blank label dropped rows. server.py wrote X-Auth-Method with an `or ""`
fallback, so the middleware read a present-but-empty header and its
"unknown" default never fired. Prometheus reads a blank label value as
absent, so those requests fell out of `sum by (method)`. The fix coerces
at emission in _emit_auth_metric and leaves the header alone: nginx
forwards it and downstream consumers read it.

Only one operator could see the mix. The heartbeat now carries
auth_path_share_24h, auth_path_volume_bucket_24h, and
auth_path_window_hours, and schema_version goes to "6". Shares, not
counts: raw per-path counts bound to a stable registry_id would make a
traffic meter. Percentages use largest-remainder rounding so they sum to
exactly 100, all three fields go None together at zero volume, and the
window clamps at 48h because the collector bounds it at le=48 and an

The collector declares the three fields and schema_version in the same

fix(search): take the raw search query out of the logs behind an opt-in flag

A search query is free text a user typed. It can hold a name, an email
address, an account number, or the name of an unannounced project. Thirteen
log lines wrote it verbatim at INFO or DEBUG, one of them next to the
username, so anyone with log access could reconstruct what individual users
searched for.

The query text now sits behind SEARCH_LOG_QUERY_TEXT, off by default. When
enabled, the registry logs it once in search(), which is the entry point for
all three repository paths, and mcpgw logs it in search_registry and
intelligent_tool_finder. Both services warn at startup so it is not left on
after a debugging session.

Redacting the query does not cost the operator the diagnostics. The token
count, candidate counts, per-type result counts, k_per_type, efSearch and
text_boost all survive, so a bad result is still explainable without the
text.

Seven sites came from reading the code. A canary test that asserts no log
record contains a nonsense query string found six more, because those
messages never contain the word "query":

  - Per-type vector search for '%s'
  - Keyword search for '%s' found %d candidates
  - Hybrid search for '%s' returned ...
  - Lexical-only search for '%s' returned ...
  - get_servers_json called: ... query={query!r}
  - list_agents called: ... query={query!r}

fix(search): grade keyword-matched tools instead of scoring every one 1.0

The keyword text-boost stage built matching_tools with a MongoDB $filter plus
$map and stamped a literal "relevance_score": 1.0 on every element. Any tool
whose name or description matched the query regex at all came back with a
perfect score, so an agent choosing the best two or three tools from a result
had nothing to rank on.

_score_tool_relevance() has computed a graded score since d97a24b6 (31 May
2026), but that fix never touched the $map. Two of the four paths that build
matching_tools were affected: the aggregation pipeline in search() and
_lexical_only_search(). DocumentDB supports $search: {vectorSearch: ...} and
MongoDB CE does not, so DocumentDB hit the flat score on every query while a
local Compose stack ran the correct Python scorer and looked fine. That is why
this survived four months.

The stage now emits no score. It selects candidate tools and Python grades
what it selected via _grade_matching_tools(), so one scorer runs on every path
and both backends. Tools scoring 0.0 are dropped rather than returned with a
meaningless number, and matching_tools is sorted best first.

text_boost is untouched, so result ordering for existing queries does not
move. Verified against the local corpus over five queries: text_boost byte
identical and the kept tool set identical, while the old stage returned
exactly [1.0] for every tool on every query.

Measured on DocumentDB after the fix, "current time in tokyo" returns 33 tool
scores across 8 servers spanning 0.31, 0.45, 0.62, 0.76 and 0.90.

Also surfaces the absolute similarity. _attach_similarity_scores() already
computed the raw cosine, but no response model declared the field so Pydantic
dropped it. relevance_score is rank-relative and maps the top hit of any query
to 1.0 by construction; similarity_score is comparable across queries and is
what a caller batching independent searches needs. Both now reach the caller
on every top-level result type. Bounded [-1.0, 1.0] because cosine is signed:
a ge=0.0 bound would 500 the whole response on a legitimate negative.

MatchingToolResult.relevance_score becomes required. Every path grades its
tools, so a missing score means a path stopped grading and should fail loudly
rather than silently report 0.0 for a tool that matched.

fix(search): offload embedding and replace the per-type vector loop with one query

Two reported causes of search latency spikes up to 1.4s, plus two defects found
while measuring them.

Cause 1: model.encode() blocked the event loop. _embed_texts() called the
synchronous, CPU-bound encode() directly inside an async def, so every other
request on the worker waited, including health checks and auth. Measured at
16.5ms p50 on all-MiniLM-L6-v2, with a 10ms heartbeat observed returning after
50.1ms. It now runs via asyncio.to_thread and the heartbeat holds at 11.0ms.

The offload is bounded by a semaphore. Torch parallelises inside a single
encode, so letting the default executor grow to min(32, cpu_count + 4) would put
dozens of encodes on the same cores and make every concurrent search slower.

Cause 2: five sequential vector queries, one per entity type. From ECS
CloudWatch timestamps the vector stage cost 59 to 885ms across five consecutive
searches, against ~16ms for the embedding, so the database dominated by 20 to
60x rather than the other way round.

The issue proposed running those five concurrently. They are deleted instead,
because they were redundant. $search selects the nearest k documents before any
$match runs, so a pipeline of $search (k=30) plus $match entity_type=skill does
not return the top 30 skills; it returns whichever of the global top 30 happen to
be skills. Every per-type pipeline ran the same global search and differed only
in what it kept. Measured on DocumentDB: four pipelines at k=30 produced 30
candidates in total, never 30 each. The loop added round trips and no recall, so
it never achieved the fair representation it was written for in #1160.

One global query now runs, with entity types filtered by a single $in and the
distribution left to _distribute_results() further down.

That also fixes a ranking defect nobody had reported.
_reciprocal_rank_fusion() treats list position as the vector rank and documents
its input as "sorted by vector similarity", but it received the per-type blocks
concatenated in loop order, sorted by text_boost within each block. Entity type
outranked similarity, and the caller's entity_types argument order changed the
results. A single query returns one list in similarity order.

Cause 3: the vector stage returned almost nothing. Because k is spent before
filtering, and nothing refills what the filters discard, the whole stage
returned 0 to 2 candidates out of a possible 120 on ECS. Two probes differing
only in status flags returned 1 candidate versus 30, which identifies the
filters as the cause rather than the corpus.

k now over-requests: min(max_results * VECTOR_SEARCH_OVERREQUEST, efSearch),
default multiplier 20. efSearch rises from 100 to 1000, the DocumentDB maximum,
since the whole traversal budget now goes to one query instead of five. Atlas
calls this the overrequest pattern and recommends at least 20x.

Over-requesting has a ceiling worth stating. Recall from post-filtering tracks
how much of the corpus k retrieves, so parity with the client-side path holds
while 1000 is a large share of the index and degrades as a registry grows past
a few thousand documents. The search now logs k, corpus size, coverage
percentage and survivor count on every query, and warns when survivors fall
below max_results while coverage is under 50%. Closing that gap properly needs
per-entity-type embedding collections, since collection is the only partition
DocumentDB offers for vector search: $search takes no filter and vector indexes
support no partial, sparse or compound options. Not done here.

Also aligns the two backends on the "tool" entity type. The DocumentDB path
stripped it, the client-side path passed it through. Harmless while no
standalone tool documents exist, a divergence the moment any do. A request for

test(search): record that vector latency tracks k, not efSearch

Sizing efSearch down for small k looked like an obvious follow-up after the
single-query change: a queue of 1000 for k=200 holds five times what the search
returns, and post-filtering discards the ordering precision that buys.

Measured on DocumentDB before writing it. The deployed code pins efSearch at
1000 and derives k from max_results, so varying max_results isolates the two
terms. If efSearch drove the cost, latency would be flat across all three rows:

  max_results=1   k=20    efSearch=1000   52ms mean
  max_results=10  k=200   efSearch=1000   61ms mean
  max_results=50  k=1000  efSearch=1000  155ms mean

It is not flat, so latency tracks k. The cost is materialising documents, each
carrying a 384-float embedding, rather than graph traversal. Scaling efSearch
would have targeted the wrong term.

So the change is not made. What lands instead is the measurement, as a comment
where the next person will reach for the same idea, and a test that pins
efSearch to the configured budget with the reasoning in its docstring.

The same run corrects an earlier reading of the single-query change. The first
five searches after deploy included a 3106ms cold start, which made the vector
stage look slower than the per-type loop it replaced. Steady state it is not:
the stage runs 40 to 98ms against 59 to 885ms before, roughly 6x better.

It also shows where the remaining latency is. The keyword $regex scan now costs
405 to 1012ms against the vector stage's 61ms, so it is the larger term and the
reporter's 1.4s cannot be closed without it. Separate work.

Refs #1751

fix(search): validate the vector tuning knobs and leave the HNSW queue headroom

Three gaps in the settings the previous commits introduced.

Clamp k to half of efSearch rather than all of it. HNSW cannot return more
candidates than its traversal queue holds, and a queue exactly the size of the
result set leaves the search no room to explore past what it has already
committed to returning, which costs recall at the tail of k. Before this,
max_results=50 produced k=1000 against efSearch=1000: zero headroom. At the
default multiplier the clamp only binds above max_results=25.

k and efSearch are otherwise independent, and the code now says so. efSearch is
a quality dial set to an absolute ceiling; k is the caller's max_results scaled
by the over-request multiplier. The min() is a clamp against a physical engine
limit, not an entanglement of the two.

Validate all three settings. vector_search_ef_search caps at 1000, which is the
DocumentDB ceiling, so a typo fails at startup instead of failing every query
at runtime. vector_search_overrequest and embeddings_encode_concurrency require
at least 1; zero or negative would have built a pipeline asking for no
candidates, or a semaphore that admits nothing.

Document them. All three were env-configurable but appeared on no deployment
surface and in no reference doc, so the escape hatch the coverage warning tells
operators to reach for ("raise VECTOR_SEARCH_OVERREQUEST") was undiscoverable
outside config.py. Added to .env.example with the reasoning, and to the
Embeddings / Vector Search group in the unified parameter reference. Helm and
Terraform operators set them through extraEnv, which is why they are not in the
chart env blocks and not in the reserved-name lists.

perf(search): run the vector and keyword queries concurrently

The last serialized round trip the reporter named. Their words: "That's up to 5
serialized round trips per search call, plus one additional collection.find()
regex keyword query afterward. None of these run concurrently."

The five per-type aggregations are gone, but the keyword query was still awaited
after the vector query completed. It never needed to be: the keyword filter is
built from the query tokens alone, and only the merge below reads the vector
results. So the two were serialized for no reason and the search paid the sum
where it could have paid the larger of the two.

Both now start before either is awaited, via asyncio.gather. Measured stage
times on DocumentDB put the saving between 32ms and 61ms per search, since it is
bounded by whichever stage is smaller:

  vector 61ms, keyword   32ms:   93ms -> 61ms
  vector 61ms, keyword 1042ms: 1103ms -> 1042ms

So this does not address the keyword scan's own cost, which is a separate
finding: a $or of seven case-insensitive regexes with no usable index, worst
case around a second when the query matches nothing and the scan cannot stop
early. That belongs in its own issue.

The regex guard moves with the query rather than being left behind. The keyword
pass is still skipped entirely when no token survives _tokenize_query(), so no
attacker-controlled pattern reaches Mongo, and a test now pins that by asserting
collection.find() is never called for a query with no usable tokens.

A second test asserts the two queries actually overlap, by counting peak
in-flight cursors rather than trusting the code shape.

Refs #1751

fix(audit): record an identifiable user for Entra OBO calls

The audit log showed the raw OIDC `sub` in the USER column for every
Entra-authenticated MCP call. `sub` is an opaque pairwise identifier, so an
administrator reviewing the trail could not tell who performed an action without
a reverse lookup they have no way to run.

The cause is a claim-shape gap. Entra ACCESS tokens — the token an OBO-capable
MCP server is called with — omit both `email` and `preferred_username`, and
`EntraIdProvider.validate_token` resolves `username` to
`preferred_username or sub`. The audit identity resolver then had no readable
claim to prefer and fell through to that `sub`.

Resolution is now `email -> preferred_username -> upn -> sub`. Both Entra token
versions are covered: v1.0 carries `upn` (the shape in the report), v2.0 carries
only `email`. Verified in production against a real Entra tenant — the USER column
now reads the caller's UPN.

Alongside the readable handle, each record persists the durable identity claims an
operator needs to correlate an opaque identifier back to a person: `subject` (the
`sub`, kept for protocol-level correlation), `canonical_id` (Entra `oid@tid`, an
immutable object id scoped to its tenant), `principal_name`, `object_id`,
`tenant_id`, and `app_id` (`appid`/`azp`, the calling application). The `name`
claim is deliberately NOT captured: a full display name adds a personal-data
category to every audit record for no investigative gain (GDPR Art. 25(2)). All
six are nullable, feed no authorization, vault or OBO decision, and are documented
as such. `canonical_id` is length-capped like every sibling, because two capped
halves would otherwise compose to twice the cap and land full-length on one stream
but truncated on another, breaking the cross-stream join the field exists for.

The identity a record carries is now provably the authenticated one. The OBO
token-mint path previously derived it from an unverified `jwt.decode` of the raw
ingress `Authorization` header. On a cookie-authenticated request that header is
never signature-checked — `/validate` validates the session cookie first and only
falls through to a bearer when no valid cookie exists — so a caller could choose
the identity written to the audit trail while still authenticating as themselves.
`/validate` now signs the resolved identity into the internal hop token it already
mints, and the mcp-proxy hop reads it from those verified claims. The forgery was
detectable but silent; it is now impossible.

The audit API can find a person by any of it. The username filter matches the
display identity or any stored claim, with the opaque identifiers matched by
equality (which can use index bounds) and the readable handles by
case-insensitive substring. Exported CSV carries the same columns.

In the UI, the event detail panel shows the claims as labelled fields rather than
only inside the raw JSON pane. They render wrapped and individually copyable
because the panel is a one-third sidebar: measured in a browser at 1024px, the
previous truncating layout showed 10 of 73 characters of `canonical_id`, and
`canonical_id` and `object_id` rendered as the identical string — so the operator
could not distinguish the two fields that exist to identify a user, which is the
issue's own "expose the associated upn/oid" requirement. The identity filter also
now states that it takes free text and searches on Enter, instead of presenting an
empty dropdown reading "No options available" beside a placeholder inviting a
paste.

`registry/audit/models.py` defines the six fields once, in `IdentityClaims`, and
both record models take their claim block from it, so the two copies cannot drift
apart again. Composition rather than inheritance: Pydantic orders base-class fields
first, which would have reordered the serialized keys of every record already
stored.

Verified: 8174 passed; `tsc --noEmit` and eslint clean; and end-to-end through the
real `EntraIdProvider` with issue #1642's exact claim shape — RS256 over mocked
JWKS, tenant-pinned issuer, closed audience allowlist — plus a live OBO
`tools/call` whose record shows the UPN, `oid@tid`, and the `sub` retained
separately.

Closes #1642

perf(audit): search only the identity fields a stream can populate

The username filter built the same five-branch `$or` for every stream. On
`registry_api_access` records four of those branches can never match: the auth
server hands the registry a thin signed assertion rather than raw IdP claims, so
`principal_name`, `subject`, `canonical_id` and `object_id` are declared on the
model but serialize as permanent nulls. That stream is both the bulk of the
collection (2556 of 2570 records on the reference deployment) and the view the
audit UI opens by default, so the filter was evaluating four dead predicates per
document scanned on the hottest path it has.

It now matches the display username alone there. No row can be lost: neither an
equality nor a regex predicate matches null.

Two comments claimed measured index-key counts that no index on this schema can
produce ("equality examined 1 index key"). Only `identity.username` is indexed;
the claim fields are not, so today every form of this filter scans. The comments
now say so, and record the reason adding those indexes will not by itself help:
MongoDB serves an `$or` by index union only when every branch is indexable, and
the two readable branches are case-insensitive regexes that never are. Isolating
the equality branches from the regex ones is the prerequisite, not the index.
Verified against the deployed DocumentDB 5.0 cluster and locally: identical plan
and identical work before and after the indexes exist, and 5200 documents
examined collapsing to 1 once the regex branches are removed.

Keeping the equality form is still correct. It stops a short filter value from
sweeping in unrelated users' records, and it is the only form an index could ever
serve.

fix(audit): stop a blank claim and a signed "anonymous" from naming a caller

Three narrow gaps in the identity a record ends up carrying.

`_claim_str` treated a whitespace-only claim as usable, because `"   "` is
truthy. A record whose principal name is three spaces identifies nobody while
looking like it does, and an operator filtering on it gets no rows and no
explanation. The value is now stripped before the emptiness test, so such a claim
degrades to None like any other unusable shape. Trimming also makes surrounding
whitespace stop breaking the equality lookup the opaque fields are searched by.

The OBO mint attributed its audit record with `obo_display or obo_principal or
"anonymous"`. `_audit_identity_display` returns the literal `"anonymous"` when no
claim identified the caller, and that string is truthy, so it won over the
verified `sub` principal: a caller we can actually name was recorded as
unattributed. The verified principal now wins. `"anonymous"` is a named constant
rather than a literal in both the producer and the consumer, since the two have to
agree for this to hold.

The absent-claim fallback was silent. It is reached legitimately mid-rolling-deploy
by an in-flight token that predates the claim, but a replica that never stamps it
at all (a marker-secret mismatch suppressing the mint, a stale task definition)
was indistinguishable from normal operation. A DEBUG line now records the fallback,
naming only the server, no identity values.

Tests cover each fix and fail without it, plus the two defensive branches in
`_claim_str` that had no coverage: rejecting a bool (`isinstance(True, int)` would
otherwise store the string "True") and exhausting a multivalued claim whose members
are all unusable.

fix(mongodb): run the init script from the image, and stop it destroying data

The `setup-mongodb` Job installed a database schema once and then never again.
Kubernetes Jobs are immutable, so `helm upgrade` on an existing install either
patched nothing — leaving the Completed Job alone, so an index added by a release
was never created — or failed outright with "field is immutable" once the pod
template changed. Either way the database kept whatever schema it was first
installed with.

Making the Job a `post-install,post-upgrade` hook fixes that, but on its own it
would have activated two destructive paths that then ran on every upgrade,
forever. Both trace to the same root cause: the chart carried its own 589-line
copy of `scripts/init-mongodb-ce.py`, because a chart cannot `.Files.Get` outside
its own directory. The copy had drifted from source in six functional ways. Two
mattered:

- Its scope seeds had transposed `group_mappings` — the regression fixed for #1574,
  where the unrestricted scopes get no groups and every administrator resolves to
  zero server access. `_load_default_scopes` upserts with `$set`, so each upgrade
  would re-apply it over the database.
- The Job's only environment was the MongoDB credential secret, which carries no
  TTL key, and the chart had no knob for one. `AUDIT_LOG_MONGODB_TTL_DAYS`
  therefore always resolved to the script's 7-day default, and the
  `IndexOptionsConflict` handler dropped and recreated the TTL at 7 days. An
  operator who had raised retention for compliance would lose everything older
  than 7 days, within about a minute, on an upgrade that said nothing.

So rather than resync the copy, delete it. The Job now runs the registry image's
own `/app/scripts/init-mongodb-ce.py`. The image already ships the script, the
scope seeds it loads from its own directory, and a uv.lock-pinned venv with
motor/pymongo — docker-compose already invoked it exactly this way. A copy cannot
drift if there is no copy, and this also removes the `pip install` of unpinned
packages that ran on every upgrade with the database credential in scope, the
`wait.py` init container (which looped with no deadline and always built a
credentialed URI, so it could never connect to a no-auth MongoDB CE), and the
second, competing mechanism for injecting the Entra admin group.

Retention becomes a Helm value, and the script now refuses to SHORTEN a TTL unless
`AUDIT_LOG_MONGODB_TTL_ALLOW_SHRINK` is set, leaving the longer window in place
and saying so. Lengthening still applies immediately.

Other correctness fixes in the same files:

- The unique-index migration now creates the composite `(request_id, log_type)`
  index BEFORE dropping the single-field one, so uniqueness is never briefly
  unenforced on a live cluster. On a pre-existing true duplicate it fails loudly
  with the aggregation that lists the offending pairs and leaves the old index in
  place, rather than half-migrating and wedging every later upgrade. That
  single-field index is why the second audit record of a request was rejected and
  logged as CRITICAL "AUDIT RECORD DROPPED" on Helm-deployed MongoDB CE.
- The blind `time.sleep(10)` and the deleted `wait.py` are replaced by a bounded
  wait in the script: wait for `ping`, then for replica-set readiness, and only
  initialize the set here after a grace period, so it cannot race the MongoDB
  Kubernetes operator into a single-member set under the wrong name.
- Identity-claim indexes are pinned per stream with a `partialFilterExpression`
  and lead with `log_type`, which every audit query filters on. Measured on a
  representative 30k-record mix: 2.09 MB across 13 pinned indexes versus 3.46 MB
  across 9 unpinned, and an insert updates 4-5 of them instead of all 9. `sparse`
  is not used — on a compound index it keeps a document when any indexed field
  exists, and `log_type` always exists, so it measured byte-identical to passing
  no option. The filter is a single-stream equality rather than an `$in` because
  Amazon DocumentDB only uses a partial index when the query predicate matches its
  filter expression.
- Index names are explicit and identical on both backends. They were previously
  auto-generated, producing different names per engine for the same logical index —
  which is why an earlier migration had to guess at name variants to drop one.
- Hook weight is -10, not 5. openbao-init is also 5, so Helm broke the tie
  alphabetically and the OpenBao bootstrap gated this database migration.
- The Job gets `activeDeadlineSeconds`, `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` and resource
  requests: it now gates the release, so an unbounded one hung `helm upgrade
  --wait` until the release timeout with the cause in a pod that the next attempt
  deleted. Helm also does not delete hook resources on uninstall.

`tests/unit/test_chart_mongodb_init_wiring.py` asserts what a byte-parity test on
a copy could not: that no chart embeds an init script, that the path the Job
executes exists, that the image ships it, that every scope file the script loads is
present, and that both backends name each claim index identically. The helm
unittest suite covers the hook, the absence of any mounted script, the retention
passthrough and the bounds; each case was falsified by reverting the behaviour it
covers.

Verified: 8113 passed; helm lint/template/unittest clean; and the migration run
against a real MongoDB from the exact pre-upgrade index state — 13 pinned indexes
created, 9 legacy dropped, the old unique index retired, both records for one
request storable, true duplicates still rejected, idempotent on a second run, and a
90-day retention preserved against a defaulted 7.

chore(release): bump the mongodb-configure image tag with every other chart

`charts/mongodb-configure` now pins `global.image.tag`, because its setup-mongodb

workflow's update loop was a hardcoded list of four values files, so that new tag

pinning `global.image.tag` appears in the update loop specifically — not merely
somewhere in the file, which the PR body would have satisfied — that the PR body

fix(mongodb): stop indexing claim fields the audit API no longer searches

`registry_api_access` records nest the identity claim fields the same way
`mcp_server_access` records do, so the claim indexes covered both streams. Since
#1774 the audit API does not search claims on that stream: the registry receives a
thin signed assertion from the auth server rather than raw IdP claims, so the
fields are permanent nulls there and matching them could only ever cost a
predicate per document for a branch that cannot hit.

Four of the thirteen claim indexes therefore served no query, on the largest
stream in the collection (2556 of 2570 records on the reference deployment) and
the one the audit UI opens by default. Dropping those targets takes the set from
13 to 9 and removes their share of per-insert index maintenance. The four are
added to LEGACY_AUDIT_CLAIM_INDEXES so a cluster that already built them has them
retired on the next run.

`AUDIT_NESTED_LOG_TYPES` becomes `AUDIT_CLAIM_NESTED_LOG_TYPES`, because the set
is no longer "streams that nest the claims" but "streams whose nested claims are
worth indexing", and `registry_api_access` still belongs to the former.

Also corrects the docstring's premise. It said each claim needs an index "or the
whole `$or` degrades to a collection scan". Adding the indexes does not stop the
scan: the identity filter is one `$or` mixing claim equality with
case-insensitive regex on the readable fields, and an `$or` is served by index
union only when every branch is indexable, which a case-insensitive regex never
is. Measured on MongoDB, adding the claim indexes left both the plan and the
documents examined unchanged, and removing the regex branches took documents
examined from 5200 to 1. What `log_type` leading every key does buy is a bound on
the stream. A seek to a claim value additionally needs the equality branches
split out of that `$or`, which is a change to the query, not the schema.

`test_registry_api_stream_gets_no_claim_index` pins the exclusion on both
backends and fails if the stream is added back or the superseded names are not
retired.

fix(audit): close two exposures on the audit path, and make degradation visible

Follow-ups from a review of the Entra OBO identity work (#1642). None of these are
required to attribute a caller, which is why they are separate — but two of them
close exposures that the identity work widens, so this should land with it or
immediately after, not later.

Two data-exposure fixes:

- `emit_audit_event` serialized the WHOLE audit record and logged it on
  `registry.audit`, which propagates to root handlers: stdout, a rotating file,
  and the `application_logs` MongoDB collection. Application logs have a different
  retention (a day by default) and a different access boundary than the audit
  collection the compliance documentation reasons about. The `username` leak
  predates this; the durable IdP identifiers (UPN, `oid`, `tid`, `appid`) are new,
  and shipping them into three extra sinks contradicts the data-minimisation
  rationale used to justify dropping the `name` claim. The record stream now goes
  to a dedicated `registry.audit.records` logger with `propagate = False` and its
  own handler, and the operator-facing payload masks the durable identifiers.
  `app_log_excluded_loggers` was NOT usable as the fix: it is only consulted by the
  MongoDB handler, so the console and file copies would still have received the
  values, and an operator can unset it. `registry.audit` itself could not be made
  terminal either — it is the parent of `registry.audit.service`, which emits the
  CRITICAL "AUDIT RECORD DROPPED" line. Full-fidelity claims remain in the durable
  audit store, which is where the audit UI and the identity feature read them.
- `_forward_headers` filtered the hop-by-hop and proxy-context header sets, but
  `x-internal-token` was in neither: it was stripped only on the vault/OBO
  branches. So for a plain registered MCP server, the gateway's own SECRET_KEY-
  signed hop JWT reached the registrant's backend — a credential replayable
  against `/mcp-proxy`, and now also a carrier of the caller's identity. It is
  stripped unconditionally, including when `relay_authorization` is set, and the
  `_EGRESS_STRIP_HEADERS` comment that claimed otherwise is corrected. The
  non-egress path had no coverage at all; it does now.

Correctness and robustness:

- `_claim_str` guarded only 2 of the 7 `_emit_token_mint_audit` call sites; a
  duplicated resolver fed the other five. `email` arrives from
  `registry/auth/dependencies.py` as `claims.get("email") or ""`, so a multivalued
  Keycloak mapper put a list into the record, `ValidationError` fired inside the
  best-effort emit, and the whole audit record was silently DROPPED. Both identity
  values are now coerced once, inside `_emit_token_mint_audit`, so every site is
  covered by construction, and the duplicated resolver is gone.
- The OBO mint record used a fresh `request_id` and a null `correlation_id`, so it
  could never be joined to the `mcp_server_access` record for the same request —
  even though the unique `(request_id, log_type)` index exists precisely so records
  of different `log_type` can share one id. `/validate` now signs its `request_id`
  into the hop claim as `rid`, and the mint record records it as `correlation_id`.
  A token minted before this change still audits.
- `_audit_provider` fell back to the configured IdP even for a `self_signed`
  token — one the gateway minted itself, which no IdP ever saw. That fallback is
  skipped now; such a token still reports the provider its originating session
  recorded.
- `_csv_safe` missed formulas behind leading whitespace or a newline. Spreadsheets
  trim a cell before deciding whether it is a formula, so `" =HYPERLINK(...)"` was
  live content in an export. The `username` query parameter was also unbounded
  while being interpolated into a regex; it is now length-limited.
- An `if audit_identity:` branch documented as "omitted when empty" could never be
  false, because the claim builder always seeds a display value. Its test passed a
  call shape no caller produces, so it would have kept passing if the branch were
  deleted. Both are gone.

Observability:

- The degradation paths were silent — an absent hop claim falling back to the
  opaque `sub`, and a claim coerced away or truncated. They now increment
  `audit_integrity_degraded_total`, labelled by a bounded `reason`, so they are
  alertable as a rate instead of invisible; the only prior signal was a
  `logger.critical` line, which cannot be alerted on as a rate. Deliberately no
  unbounded label dimensions: no tenant, app, principal or request id as an
  attribute. An ABSENT claim counts nothing — normal for any IdP that omits it —
  which is what keeps the series meaningful.
- The Status Distribution card is hidden for the `token_mint` stream, which
  structurally has no `response.status_code` to bucket, rather than rendering a
  titled card containing "No data available".

Verified: 8221 passed. Both exposure fixes re-proved independently of their own
tests — a record's six claim values reach the durable store intact and no root
handler (re-enabling propagation leaks them again, so the guard is load-bearing),
and no `x-internal-token` variant survives `_forward_headers` on the non-egress
path.

masked them in the operator-facing copy, on the grounds that stdout is scraped
into the same store. It left the display `username` verbatim so the stream stays
readable.

    "principal_name": "[REDACTED]"

commonest case, while the data-minimisation argument used to justify it (and to
justify not storing the `name` claim at all) applies to `username` equally.
