than "above" (it is declared in the auth server's meters module, not that file).

Enforce list_skills discovery gate on single-skill read and catalog surfaces

Skill authorization is two-layered: a type-level list_skills discovery grant,
then a per-record visibility check. The listing path and semantic-search branch
enforce both, but several single-record read surfaces enforced only visibility.
Because skill visibility defaults to PUBLIC, an authenticated caller with an
empty list_skills grant could read and enumerate skills outside their discovery
scope, including the credentialed skill-content route.

Apply the shared user_has_asset_permission("skill", "list", ...) gate, before
the visibility check, to:

- _user_can_access_skill, the access check behind all eight single-skill
  read/consume routes (metadata, content, integrity, health, tools, rating,
  security-scan, rate).
- the ARD catalog search and browse skill branches, reaching parity with their
  server and agent branches. The browse gate keys on the canonical skill name
  (SkillCard.name), matching the key the grant uses.

The gate fails closed (missing/empty grant or no context denies) and leaves
admins and holders of an "all" grant unaffected.

fix: enforce OBO egress target-audience/scope allowlist on live paths

The on-behalf-of egress audience/scope rules were implemented only in the
ServerInfo model validator, which is never constructed on the live request
paths, so the configure write path enforced only the gateway-own-audience
check and the token-vend path returned stored directives unvalidated.

Extract the audience/scope floor into a shared validator and wire it into
both live paths, fail-closed:

- Write path (configure egress auth): reject with 400 any obo directive whose
  target audience is missing, malformed, the gateway's own app, not an allowed
  internal audience, or whose scopes are not bound to the target, before it can
  be persisted.
- Vend path (internal egress token): re-validate the stored directive and
  refuse with 403 if it no longer passes, so directives predating this
  enforcement cannot be exchanged for a delegated token to a disallowed
  audience.

The model validator now delegates to the same function, giving a single source
of truth. Adds write-path and vend-path tests covering the rejected and
accepted cases.

Forward only allowlisted headers to the external registration gate

The registration-gate admission-control service copied inbound request
headers into the payload POSTed to the operator-configured external gate,
excluding only a three-name denylist. Credential-bearing headers owned by
the registry and gateway (the caller's bearer x-authorization and the signed
internal service token x-internal-token-registry) were not on that denylist
and were disclosed in cleartext to the third-party gate on every register or
update.

Rebuild the outbound header set from an explicit allowlist of non-credential
context headers instead of a denylist, so any credential or internal identity
header is dropped by default and cannot leak if new such headers are added
later. Matching is case-insensitive, and the allowlist is re-applied as a
backstop immediately before serialization so a directly constructed request
cannot reintroduce a stripped header.

Enforce per-caller tool visibility on server.json export and virtual-server tool listing

The canonical server.json export and the virtual-server tool listing returned
MCP tool metadata without the per-caller tool-visibility filter that every
other single-server read surface applies. A caller granted a server (or virtual
server) but only a subset of its tools could recover the full tool inventory —
names, descriptions, input schemas, backend server paths, and required scopes.

Canonical export (GET /api/servers/{path}/server.json): apply the shared
_apply_tool_visibility helper before projecting to canonical form, so the
_meta tool_list and num_tools are pruned to the caller's allowlist. Same helper
used by GET /api/servers/{path} and get_server_details.

Virtual-server tool listing (GET /api/virtual-servers/{path}/tools): thread the
caller context into resolve_tools/_resolve_tool_list and apply three fail-closed
layers matching the tool-catalog surface and the data-plane scope gate:
skip backends the caller cannot access (user_can_access_server_from_doc),
prune surviving tools through filter_tools_for_user, and drop tools whose
required_scopes the caller lacks.

All layers fail closed (missing context / empty grant / insufficient scope ->
no tools); admins and wildcard grants pass through unchanged.

Harden IdP bootstrap against default credentials

Remove all shipped default and weak credentials from the identity-provider
bootstrap paths, make them fail closed, and stop granting the Keycloak web
client wildcard CORS origins or a wildcard post-logout allowlist.

PingFederate bootstrap (pingfederate/setup/init-pingfederate.sh):
- Require PF_ADMIN_PASS, PINGFEDERATE_CLIENT_SECRET and the new
  PF_REGISTRY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from the environment with no fallback values.
- Add a fail-closed validator that rejects unset, empty, whitespace-only,
  known-weak (denylisted, after trimming) and too-short credentials before
  anything is created, and writes the trimmed value back so what was validated
  is what gets transmitted.
- Seed only a single admin login, drop the relaxed password policy, remove the
  hardcoded demo users, and rotate a pre-existing weak admin password on re-run.
- Verify every admin-API response status and abort on non-2xx, echoing the
  response body so a password-policy rejection is distinguishable from a
  malformed payload.
- Build the OAuth client payload with a JSON serializer from the environment so
  the stored secret matches the validated value and special characters are safe.
- Exit non-zero without printing a success banner when the idp_user_groups seed
  fails; that state authenticates but is denied every action.
- Stop printing credential values.

Keycloak mcp-gateway-web client, in all four provisioners
(keycloak/import/realm-config.json, keycloak/setup/init-keycloak.sh,
charts/keycloak-configure/templates/configmap.yaml,
terraform/aws-ecs/scripts/init-keycloak.sh):
- Remove the "+" wildcard webOrigins entry. WebOriginsUtils.resolveValidWebOrigins
  expands it to the origin of every redirect URI, so CORS widened silently
  whenever a redirect was added. Nothing needed it: the browser only performs
  top-level navigations to Keycloak and the auth-server does the code exchange
  server-side over internal DNS.
- Set an explicit "##"-delimited post.logout.redirect.uris allowlist. An absent
  or "+" attribute makes getPostLogoutRedirectUris fall back to the union of
  redirectUris, which includes the auth-server OAuth callback.
- Give keycloak/setup/init-keycloak.sh the 409->PUT client upsert the other two
  provisioners already had. A bare POST 409s on a re-run, so these changes would
  otherwise never reach an existing realm while the script reported success.
- Apply realm settings to an EXISTING realm in all three provisioners. Each one
  treated a positive existence probe, and a 409, as "nothing to do", so a
  realm-level setting would never reach a deployment whose realm predates the
  change. The settings body is now declared before the existence check and PUT to
  /admin/realms/{realm} when the realm is already there; a failed update aborts
  instead of continuing.
- Let the caller's environment win over .env in keycloak/setup/init-keycloak.sh for
  KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_URL, REGISTRY_URL and AUTH_SERVER_EXTERNAL_URL, and have
  infra/scripts/post-deploy.sh export them. Keycloak replaces redirectUris and
  webOrigins wholesale on a client PUT, so once an existing client is updated
  rather than skipped, a host that already has a Compose .env would otherwise have
  had its loopback values written over a deployed realm; KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_URL is
  included because a stale .env would retarget the whole run at a local Keycloak.
  post-deploy.sh previously exported nothing and wrote .env only when absent.
- Send sslRequired only when CREATING the Helm realm, never on update. It is
  null-guarded in Keycloak's updateRealm, so omitting it preserves whatever the
  realm has; including it in the update body would revert an operator who hardened
  it to "external" on every helm upgrade. Harmless while the body was create-only.
- Drop the duplicate "print the response body" realm POST from all three
  provisioners: re-sending a create to obtain an error body is a second create
  attempt that can succeed on a transient failure. The newly-fatal realm and
  client writes now capture the body alongside the status and print it, so a 4xx
  names the rejected field instead of reporting a bare code.
- Use `curl -sS` without discarding stderr in pf_api, so a refused admin port
  reports curl's reason rather than a bare "HTTP 000". Step 1 waits on the
  runtime port, not the admin port, so that is a realistic first failure.
- Fail loudly on the remaining silent client-update paths: the Helm upsert no
  longer accepts POST 409 as success (it re-resolves the id and PUTs), and the
  ECS provisioner returns non-zero when the client id cannot be resolved or the
  PUT is rejected, instead of printing success.
- Enable bruteForceProtected, with failureFactor 5 and a 60s wait increment, on
  the three realms that are actually provisioned; the descriptor already set it
  but is never imported. Note this makes the seeded admin lockable after five
  failed logins.
- Set fullScopeAllowed: false on both mcp-gateway-web and mcp-gateway-m2m in all
  three provisioners. Omitting it takes Keycloak's default of true, which puts
  every role the user holds into the token, including other clients' roles:
  verified on a live realm that granting a user realm-management:manage-users made
  resource_access["realm-management"] appear in an mcp-gateway-web access token,
  so a gateway-scoped token was replayable against Keycloak's own Admin API. With
  the flag set, realm_access and resource_access come back empty and the token is
  355 bytes smaller. The descriptor already specified false; that intent had never
  reached a running deployment. Nothing here authorizes on roles -- authorization
  is group-driven through the groups mapper -- so this removes the exposure without
  changing behaviour.
- Keep sslRequired: none in the Helm realm body on update as well as create. That
  topology reaches Keycloak over plain HTTP on the in-cluster service address, and
  "external" makes Keycloak answer "HTTPS required" because the EKS pod CIDR is not
  treated as private, breaking the token and admin calls the Job itself makes; TLS
  terminates at the ALB. Compose and ECS still omit the field so an operator's
  hardened value survives an upgrade there.

Keycloak realm descriptor (keycloak/import/realm-config.json):
- Remove the shipped credential entirely. Realm import has no fail-closed path
  for a password: StringPropertyReplacer re-emits an unresolved placeholder
  verbatim and RepresentationToModel.createCredentials stores that literal text

fix(cimd): quote CIMD_CLIENT_NAME in .env.example

`build_and_run.sh` sources `.env` (four call sites: lines 227, 264, 406, 636), so
an unquoted value containing spaces is parsed as an assignment followed by a
command. Copying `.env.example` to `.env` and running the script failed with:

    .env: line NNN: Registry: command not found

and, had it continued, would have set CIMD_CLIENT_NAME to just "AI".

Every other space-containing value in the file is already quoted

REGISTRY_DESCRIPTION="..."); this was the only one that was not.

The other three surfaces are unaffected: the compose files interpolate

(verified with `docker compose config`, which resolves it to the full string),
Helm already quotes it in values.yaml, and the Terraform default is an HCL string.

test(env): make .env.example shell-safety enforceable in CI

The documented first step of a local deployment is `cp .env.example .env`, and
build_and_run.sh then does `source .env` (four call sites). The shell, not a
dotenv parser, is what reads this file first, so a value the shell mis-parses
breaks the very first command a new user runs. Nothing checked that.

`CIMD_CLIENT_NAME=AI Registry Tools` shipped unquoted and bash read it as
"assign CIMD_CLIENT_NAME=AI, then run `Registry` with argument `Tools`":

    .env: line 1408: Registry: command not found

Three checks, each catching it from a different angle, because the failure has
two halves and the loud one is easier:

- every value containing whitespace is quoted. Names the line and key, so the
  fix is obvious rather than inferred.
- `bash -c 'source .env.example'` exits 0 with empty stderr. Covers the whole
  class, including backticks, $(...) and unbalanced quotes that the targeted
  check would miss.
- values survive the round trip. `CIMD_CLIENT_NAME` sourced to "" rather than
  "AI Registry Tools", and a value that parses while losing its tail is the
  quieter half: it looks plausible and fails later, somewhere else.

Verified load-bearing: reverting the quotes fails all three, and the second
reproduces the operator-visible error verbatim.

The convention already existed (REGISTRY_NAME, REGISTRY_ORGANIZATION_NAME and
REGISTRY_DESCRIPTION are all quoted) and one line missed it. This makes it
enforced rather than remembered.

Two notes for whoever refreshes this next:

- Generate with `ensure_ascii=True` (the json.dumps default) and `indent=2`. The
  committed file escapes non-ASCII as `\uXXXX`; writing literal characters
  instead rewrites every em-dash in every docstring and buries the real change in
  27 lines of noise.
- The registry container must be built from the commit being documented. The
  build used here predated main's tip by one commit, which was verified harmless
  because that commit touched only a handler body, tests and docs, with no
  decorator, signature, `response_model` or `status_code` change, so the
  generated schema is identical.

docs: make the openapi.json refresh a checked step, not a remembered one

`api/openapi.json` is the published API contract and it is hand-refreshed: no
script generates it, no CI job checks it. So a PR can add a route, pass every
gate, and leave the new endpoint invisible to API consumers. That is not
hypothetical: when #1711 added `GET /oauth/client-metadata.json`, the committed
spec was ALSO still missing audit-endpoint changes from three earlier merged PRs,
so it had been silently stale for a while.

Three places now cover it.

CLAUDE.md gains a "Regenerating api/openapi.json" section with the procedure and
the four ways it goes wrong, ordered by how easy each is to miss:

- Do not pass `ensure_ascii=False`. The committed file escapes non-ASCII as
  \uXXXX, so writing literal characters rewrites every em-dash in every docstring
  and turns a 9-line change into 56 insertions and 28 deletions.
- Set `info.version` by hand. The live app reports a git-describe development
  string (`1.30.0-46-g...`), never a release version.
- Build the container from the commit being documented, with the escape hatch:
  if it is behind, confirm no changed file altered a route decorator, signature,
  `response_model` or `status_code`, since a changed handler body cannot affect
  the schema.
- Diff semantically, not by eye. An 824 KB JSON file hides accidental removals,
  which usually mean the container ran with a feature flag off or the wrong
  DEPLOYMENT_MODE, so a whole router never registered.

The recipe in that section was verified to reproduce the committed artifact
byte-for-byte rather than written from memory.

The pr-review skill gains Step 2.6, which detects an added route decorator and
blocks when the spec was not refreshed, plus a reporting table alongside the
existing config-parameter one. The detector matches ANY router object rather than

completely, which I only found by running it against that PR. Verified to fire on

fix(security): stop search_registry tripping the credential-harvesting rule, and release stale blocks

Two problems, found by rescanning the gateway's own MCP server.

1. search_registry was auto-blocked HIGH:CREDENTIAL HARVESTING.

Cisco's credential_harvesting.yara carries an unconditional clause:

    $mcp_credential_patterns = /\b(claude_desktop_config\.json|...)\b/i
    condition: ... or $mcp_credential_patterns or ...

Every other clause in that rule needs a credential pattern AND an action verb AND
passes a `not $generic_config_ops` guard. That one needs nothing, so merely naming
claude_desktop_config.json anywhere in a tool description is an automatic HIGH.

The docstring named it once, as an example of where a user adds a discovered
server. Checked all four unconditional patterns against the exact description the
scanner saw: only that literal matched, exactly once. The heuristic is reasonable
in general, since that file holds MCP server credentials; this was a false
positive because the tool only mentions it, never touches it.

Reworded to "add it to your MCP client's server configuration". Same information
for the model, no credential-file reference. Verified the rewritten docstring
matches none of the rule's credential patterns, and grepped the repo: the literal
appears in no other tool description.

2. A passing scan never released a block it no longer reproduced.

Reconciliation ran only when a scan came back UNSAFE. So once the reworded tool
scanned clean, the stale auto-block would have survived every future rescan, with
no way to clear it short of an admin override. A one-line false positive would
have become permanent.

Both scan paths now reconcile on a safe scan too. Scan-sourced entries are
rebuilt from the current scan, so one that is no longer flagged is dropped, while
admin decisions are preserved. Deliberately NOT via _apply_unsafe_scan_decision:
that disables the server when nothing is blocked, which on a passing scan would be
backwards.

feat(auth): OAuth 2.1 discovery identity for backend-authenticated MCP servers

Issue #966 asks for the registry's headless calls -- health checks, tool discovery,
security scans -- to authenticate as the registry rather than reusing whatever
credential happens to be configured for end-user traffic. This adds that identity
and a three-tier resolver that decides which credential a headless call presents.

`registry/core/backend_oauth.py` is the single entry point: `with_bearer(server_info)`
resolves at most one credential and stashes it under `RESOLVED_BEARER_KEY`, so the
synchronous header builders in mcp_client, health and the scanner path never have to
become async. Precedence, fail-closed at every step:

  1. a designated OAuth 2.1 discovery identity (per-user, consented once by an
     owner-or-admin, vaulted, refreshed lazily on vend)
  2. a client_credentials token minted from the server's own backend-auth config
  3. for obo_exchange servers only, a gateway app-only client_credentials token --
     a fallback, so an explicit `auth_scheme` always wins over it

An operator's explicit static `auth_scheme` (bearer / api_key) is never shadowed by
a derived credential. Tiers 2 and 3 bow out unless the scheme is `none`.

Credentials are bound at the moment of consent and re-checked on every vend: to the
upstreams registered at consent time, and to the token endpoint they were minted
against. Repointing `proxy_pass_url` or a custom token URL forces re-consent rather
than shipping the credential somewhere new. The cache is keyed on a fingerprint that
includes the upstream and the encrypted secret, so an edited config or a rotated
SECRET_KEY re-acquires instead of serving a stale token, and a single-flight lock
collapses concurrent resolution to one token request.

The vault gives discovery its own address space, disjoint from the per-user egress
space. That is what keeps the two apart: a user's own runtime credential and the
identity the registry borrowed are different concerns that share a principal, a
provider and a server, so one shared address would make every interaction between
them a special case -- collision on write, cross-purpose reads, reclassification on
refresh. `keys.namespaced_prefix` returns the prefix UNCHANGED for egress, so entries
written before purposes existed keep their exact addresses: no migration, no
re-consent. Discovery nests one segment deeper, inside the configured prefix so
existing OpenBao policies and IAM scoping still apply untouched. Depth alone makes
collision impossible -- egress is always four segments past the prefix, discovery
five -- and the one auth_method whose encoding could equal the purpose segment is
rejected by the per-user denylist.

`list_for_user` reads the egress space only, so a borrowed identity never appears in
the user's Connected Accounts, where a self-service disconnect would have silently
broken discovery. Removing a designation goes through the server's discovery config.

Authorization and disclosure:

  - configuring backend auth or a discovery designation is owner-or-admin; the
    designation records the CONSENTING principal, canonicalized to the vault's own
    auth_method so the address it names is one the vault can actually hold
  - re-saving a server preserves an existing designation rather than silently
    re-pointing it at whoever saved last, and a change that would strand the vaulted
    token is refused with a 409 naming the remedy instead of leaving an entry nothing
    reads
  - every read surface that returns a server record strips the backend-auth config
    for non-owners: the dedicated GETs, `GET /servers/{path}`, and the `/all` branch,
    which returns every server and gated only on server access
  - switching `auth_scheme` genuinely clears the credential fields it invalidates.
    A `{"$set": doc}` merge cannot express deletion, so the edit routes call
    `remove_server_fields` for a real `$unset` rather than popping keys from an
    in-memory dict and leaving the stored ciphertext behind to reactivate later
  - the security scanner authenticates through the same `with_bearer` chain, so it
    validates its destination before resolving a credential

A decryption failure fails closed rather than silently downgrading a confidential
client to a public-client request against the operator's real token endpoint, and
the freshness check keeps a floor so a token cannot expire between the check and the
upstream reading the header.

Tests: 76 new functions. The address carries the purpose in every store fake, so a
fake cannot pass while modelling one shared space. Covers tier precedence and each
bow-out, destination and token-endpoint binding, single-flight, the freshness floor
and its mutation, designation preservation and the stranding refusal, the read-side
redaction on all three surfaces including `/all`, the CSRF contract for the three new

fix(discovery): revoke the borrowed credential when the designation is cleared, correct the vault doc

Two defects a purpose-namespaced vault introduced or left behind.

DELETE /oauth-discovery cleared the designation and left the vaulted access and
refresh token in place, permanently. `disconnect` was hard-coded to the egress
space, so the discovery space had write and read paths but no delete path at all.
The residue is worse than an ordinary orphan: it is a live delegated credential
for a real person, and it is deliberately absent from that person's Connected
Accounts (list_for_user reads egress only), so they cannot revoke it either.
Server deletion did not reach it, nor did user offboarding.

`disconnect` now takes `purpose` as a required keyword with no default -- the same
rule the vend follows, and for the same reason: a default is how a caller ends up
pinned to one space by omission, which is how this hole opened. The DELETE handler
captures the designation before clearing it, since that is the only record of which
address holds the token, and rebuilds the address from the DESIGNATION's principal
rather than the caller's, because an admin may revoke on someone else's behalf.
Best-effort and idempotent: a designation may never have been consented, and a
vault failure must not block an operator from completing the revocation -- the
designation is already gone either way -- but it is logged loudly.

The user-facing Connected Accounts disconnect is pinned to egress, so a user cannot
revoke a discovery designation, which is an owner/admin concern.

Both discovery routes now invalidate the resolver cache. Tier 2 is uncached today,
so only tier 1 is affected, but leaving it out makes adding tier-2 caching a silent
stale-credential bug.

docs/egress-credential-vault.md still described the purpose-as-payload design this
branch replaced: a section headed 'The key carries no consent purpose', claiming
both purposes resolve to one address and that the callback refuses a cross-client
overwrite with an error string that exists nowhere in the code. That is shipped
documentation promising operators a guard that does not exist, and describing a
collision that cannot happen. Rewritten to describe the two address spaces, why
egress addresses are unchanged, and how to remove a borrowed identity.

Tests: disconnect is parametrized over both purposes to pin that it reaches its own
space and leaves the other standing. Four route-level tests cover the revoke, the
principal it addresses, the vault-failure path, and the never-consented case.
Mutation-checked: removing the revoke call, aiming it at egress, and rebuilding the
address from the caller each fail. 7424 passed.

docs(discovery): state which identity providers backend discovery supports

The Entra app-registration recipe and both Keycloak constraints were already

Only entra and keycloak are implemented; the shipped default is cognito, which

fix(discovery): keep the scan credential out of argv, name an unconfigured oauth scheme

The scan credential no longer appears on a command line. `mcp-scanner remote` only
accepts one as `--bearer-token` / `--header`, both of which land in the child's argv
and are readable by anything that can see `ps` or /proc/<pid>/cmdline for the life
of the scan. That was tolerable while the value was an operator's static scan token.
It is not now that the resolver can hand over a delegated HUMAN OAuth token -- a
borrowed discovery identity -- or the gateway's own app-only token: argv needs no
key and no decryption, so it is a far lower bar than the vault those come from.

The scanner is now launched via a small in-process shim (`python -c`) that pops the
credential from the environment and re-attaches mcp-scanner's own flag inside the
child, then hands off to the same entry point the console script uses. The
environment was already this subprocess's channel for secrets
(MCP_SCANNER_LLM_API_KEY), so this follows the existing convention rather than
inventing one; /proc/<pid>/environ is restricted to the same uid, unlike cmdline,
and `ps` never renders it. The subprocess boundary, its timeout and its output
parsing are unchanged.

An `oauth` scheme with no usable `backend_oauth` is now reported by name instead of
probed. Registration is two-step -- POST the server, then PUT /oauth-config -- so a
failed or abandoned second step leaves this state legitimately; the server was then
probed every cycle to produce a generic transport error, with the real cause only in
a log line. Note the reason reaches the stored status and logs but NOT API responses:
`_normalize_health_status` collapses every `unhealthy: *` to `unhealthy`, as it does
for all reasons today. Surfacing it to an operator needs a reason channel on the
health API, which is a separate change.

Tests pin the boundary the borrow depends on: the discovery credential is for
listing tools, health and scanning, never for executing a tool. That holds today
because execute never enters this app -- nginx proxies `tools/call` and forwards the
caller's own Authorization header -- but nothing enforced it, so three tests assert
the runtime data plane never references the resolver, that `with_bearer`'s consumers
are only the three discovery call sites, and that no tool-invocation function exists
to leak into. A future execute path will fail them rather than inherit a credential.

docs(discovery): state the scope limits and operational constraints of backend discovery

Scope:
- "Discovery" is not OAuth metadata discovery. Nothing fetches RFC 9728
  protected-resource metadata or RFC 8414 authorization-server metadata, reads a
  WWW-Authenticate challenge, or performs DCR (ADR 0001). It means the registry's own
  health / tools-list / scan calls can authenticate to a server that requires OAuth;
  the operator supplies the endpoints.
- A borrowed OAuth 2.1 identity needs EGRESS_AUTH_ENABLED, a secret store and gateway
  mode, because it lives in the per-user vault. A registry-only deployment has none of
  it. Tier 2 (client_credentials from the server's own config) has no such requirement.

Operational constraints:
- Runtime Keycloak OBO is not implemented either (_keycloak_exchange_body raises), so
  obo_exchange is Entra-only end to end, not just for discovery.
- Tier 2 is uncached, so every health cycle is a fresh secret-store read plus a token
  request -- a billed, throttleable API call per server per cycle on Secrets Manager.
- A token_url whose host RESOLVES private is accepted at config time and refused at
  use, because config-time validation runs with resolve=False to stay DNS-independent.
  Names the symptom and says why relaxing the guard is not the fix.
- `resource` is not the Entra spelling. Tier 2 sends RFC 8707 `resource` when set;
  Entra v2 wants scope=<App ID URI>/.default and ignores it.

fix(discovery): revoke on server delete, bind purpose into the AEAD, refuse Keycloak

1. DELETING A SERVER ORPHANED THE BORROWED CREDENTIAL. Clearing a designation via
DELETE /oauth-discovery revoked the vaulted token; deleting the server did not. The
residue is not a recoverable orphan -- discovery entries are deliberately absent from
the consenting user's Connected Accounts, the user-facing disconnect is pinned to the
egress purpose, and the designation recording the vault address dies with the
document -- so a real person's access and refresh tokens stayed live with nothing able
to find them. The revoke now lives in `ServerService.remove_server`, not the routes,
because EIGHT call sites reach it: two API routes plus six federation and
reconciliation paths. Fixing the routes would have covered two. It reads the
designation with include_credentials before anything is deleted, since the block is
stripped otherwise and the revoke would silently no-op.

2. THE PURPOSE SEPARATION WAS PATH-ONLY, NOT CRYPTOGRAPHIC. `CredentialCodec._aad`
bound the vault address but not `purpose`, even though purpose became part of that
address. This codec's threat model explicitly includes a write-capable attacker on the
backend -- that is what `require_encrypted` defends against -- and under exactly that
model such an attacker could copy a user's egress ciphertext to the discovery address
and have the registry borrow the user's own runtime credential for its headless calls.
The tag now covers purpose, so the copy is rejected in BOTH directions.

The segment is appended only for non-egress purposes, so every envelope written before
purposes existed -- all of which are egress -- keeps a byte-identical AAD and still
authenticates. Same rule as `keys.namespaced_prefix`, same reason: no migration, no
re-consent. Verified by asserting the egress AAD equals the pre-purpose form exactly.

3. KEYCLOAK MINTED A TOKEN IT COULD NOT AUDIENCE. `_obo_discovery_scopes` sends no
scope for Keycloak, relying on a server-side audience mapper that neither the charts
nor the realm bootstrap create. The HTTPS guard then told the operator to "set an
externally reachable HTTPS Keycloak URL to use obo_exchange discovery" -- and following
that advice got them past the guard and minted a real token audienced to whatever
Keycloak defaults to, sent to a third-party MCP server as Authorization: Bearer with
nothing downstream re-checking it. `_gateway_idp_client` now refuses Keycloak outright
and says why. The test that asserted the old behaviour is inverted; it was pinning the
vulnerability.

4. ENTRA_LOGIN_BASE_URL WAS UNSETTABLE ON THE STANDALONE REGISTRY CHART. It was added
to reserved-env-names.txt, which blocks extraEnv, but only the umbrella stack chart and
auth-server render it -- so on a standalone registry chart an operator had no way to set
it at all. Now rendered from `entra.loginBaseUrl`, declared in values, and omitted when
empty. Verified by rendering both cases.

5. The docs contradicted the code on tier numbering: two notes called tier 1 "tier 2",
and the tier-2 sizing note pointed at `oauth`-scheme servers when tier 2 applies to
`auth_scheme: none` servers carrying a designation. A runbook reader would have gone to
the wrong knob. The tier numbers are now stated explicitly against `with_bearer`.

fix(vault): honour purpose in the Secrets Manager read-repair, correct the Keycloak docs

The read-repair path on the one-document-per-principal backend was still pinned to the
egress purpose. `get_token` had `purpose` in scope and dropped it, and `_migrate`
hardcoded `keys.EGRESS_PURPOSE` for both the document name and the re-encrypt. OpenBao
threaded it correctly; this backend did not.

Encryption is OFF by default, so the ordinary upgrade path is: entries exist in
plaintext, an operator sets a key, and each read lazily re-encrypts. Under that path a
DISCOVERY entry was never repaired, so a delegated human token stayed plaintext at rest
indefinitely with nothing reporting it. Worse, `_migrate` took the principal mutation
lease on the USER'S EGRESS document -- waiting up to the lease timeout -- before
comparing against an entry that was never there, then no-oped. Tier 2 is uncached, so
that happened once per designated server per health cycle and contended with that user's
own egress writes.

Docs: `docs/obo-token-exchange.md` contradicted the code and itself. Two sections still
described Keycloak as supported-with-two-blockers, listed a remediation path that no
longer changes behaviour, and quoted a log line that no longer exists -- while a later
section correctly said it is refused outright. Rewritten to state the refusal, why it is
unconditional rather than gated on HTTPS, and what following the old advice used to do.
The activation contract now includes the `auth_scheme: none` precondition it omitted.

review: unbreak the boundary tests, surface the new setting, document the UI flow

Four items from the review and live testing of this PR. No behaviour change.

1. The two tests enforcing "a discovery credential cannot reach tool execution"
   fail on any developer machine with a virtualenv under auth_server/.

Both walk the tree with rglob("*.py") and exclude nothing, so they scan installed

`call_tool`, so both assertions fire on library code: ~23k files on a machine with

run passed honestly.

These two tests are the only enforcement of the boundary, and one says in its own
docstring "If this fails, someone added tool invocation to the app". A guard that
cries wolf locally is a guard the next person loosens until it is quiet.

Added `_is_vendored` and applied it to both walks. Verified both directions: the

with_bearer` to auth_server/server.py still fails the first one.

"How Credentials Are Used -> Health Checks" listed `bearer` and `api_key` with
